3.q:
Read the given passage carefully and answer the following questions:
            The classical realist theory of international relations has long dominated both academic institutions
     and the American government. Even at the birth of the nation, early political thinkers, such as Alexander
     Hamilton, promoted a realist view of international relations and sought to influence the actions of the
     government based on this perspective. While the classical realist school of international relations is
     not entirely homogeneous in nature, there are certain premises that all classical realists share. The
     primary principle underlying classical realism is a concern with issues of war and peace. Specifically,
     classical realists ask, what are the causes of war and what are the conditions of peace? The members
     of the classical realist school mainly attribute war and conflict to what is termed the security dilemma.
     In the absence of any prevailing global authority, each nation is required to address its own security
     needs. However, each nation’s quest for security—through military build ups, alliances, or territorial
     defences— necessarily unsettles other nations. These nations react to feelings of insecurity by engaging
     in their own aggressive actions, which leads other nations to react similarly, perpetuating the cycle. It
     is important to note that for realists, unlike idealists or liberal internationalists, international conflict is
     a necessary consequence of the structural anarchy that nations find themselves in. Whereas other
     schools may see international conflict as the result of evil dictators, historical chance, flawed socio-


   political systems, or ignorance of world affairs, classical realists see war as the logical result of a
   system that by its nature lacks a true central authority. Hand in hand with this view of conflict as an
   inevitable condition of the global power structure is the realists’ view of the nation as a unitary actor.
   Because classical realists see international relations as a continuing struggle for dominance, the nation
   cannot be viewed as a collection of individuals with disparate wants, goals, and ideologies. The
   realist view requires the formulation of a national interest, which in its simplest terms refers to the
   nation’s ability to survive, maintain its security, and achieve some level of power relative to its
   competitors. Realism is not without its critics, many of whom challenge the premise that war is the
   natural condition of international relations or that there can be a truly national interest. However, the
   realist school of international relations continues to shape foreign policy because of the successes it
   has had in describing real world interactions between nations.
   Questions :
    (a) The formation of a national interest serves what function in the classical realist theory of war
        and peace, based on the passage?                                                             (5)
    (b) What argument would members of the classical realist school would be least likely to support?(5)
    (c) What will best support the classical realist theory of international conflict?               (5)
    (d) What is the underlying principle of classic realism?                                         (5)

(b) Realists would reject the claim that conflict is merely accidental or can be eliminated by removing a few bad leaders. (c) Reciprocal military build-ups and defensive alliances that increase other states’ insecurity illustrate the security dilemma. (d) The central concern is the causes of war and conditions of peace within a system lacking a prevailing global authority.

            The cinema is an outstanding wonder of this modern age. Apart from the great pleasure it gives
     us as a means of entertainment, it is in many ways an education itself, and no regular patron of the
     cinema can be called illiterate. The cinema is also a very valuable asset to educationists. The film

     activity of many kinds of germs and their effect on water, milk or blood. We can watch the opening

1.q:
Write a précis of the following passage in about one third of its length : (10)

The great advantage of early rising is the good start it gives us in our day’s work. The early riser
has done a large amount of hard work before other men have gotten out of bed. In the early morning
the mind is fresh, and there are few sounds or other distractions, so that work done at that time is
generally well done. In many cases the early riser also finds time to take some exercise in the fresh
morning air, and this exercise supplies him with a fund of energy that will last until the evening. By
beginning so early, he knows that he has plenty of time to do thoroughly all the works he can be
expected to do, and is not tempted to hurry over any part of it. All his works being finished in good
time, he has a long interval of rest in the evening before the timely hour when he goes to bed. He gets
to sleep several hours before midnight, at the time when sleep is most refreshing and after a sound
night’s rest, rises early next morning in good health and spirits for the labours of a new day.

It is very plain that such a life as this is far more conducive to health than that of the man who
shortens his waking hours by rising late, and so can afford in the course of the day little leisure for
necessary rest. Any one who lies in bed late, must, if he wishes to do a full day’s work, go on working
to a correspondingly late hour, and deny himself the hour or two of evening exercise that he ought to
take for the benefit of his health. But, in spite of all his efforts, he will probably produce as good
results as the early riser, because he misses the best working hours of the day.

It may be objected to this that some find the perfect quiet of midnight by far the best time for
working. This is no doubt true in certain cases. Several great thinkers have found by experience that
their intellect is clearest, and they can write best, when they burn the midnight oil. But even in such
cases the practice of working late at night cannot be commended. Few men, if any, can exert the full
power of their intellect at the time when nature prescribes sleep, without ruining their health thereby;
and of course the injury done to the health must in the long run have a bad effect on the quality of the

work done.
1.explanation: Suggested title: Advantages of Early Rising. Write about one third of the original length. Retain the author’s central claims about a fresh mind, productive mornings, exercise, adequate time, evening rest and the long-term health cost of late-night work. Note that the printed sentence “he will probably produce as good results … because he misses the best working hours” is internally inconsistent; summarise the overall argument without adding a new claim.

2.q:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions that follows :

Computers are capable of doing extremely complicated work in all branches of learning. They
can solve the most complex mathematical problems or put a thousand unrelated data in order. These
machines can be put to varied uses. For instance, they can provide information on the best way to
prevent traffic accidents. They work accurately and at high speed. They save research workers’
years of hard work.

This whole process, by which machines can be used to work for us, has been called ‘automation’.
In future, automation may enable human beings to enjoy more leisure than they do today. The coming

of automation is bound to have important social consequences,


Some years ago, an expert on automation, Sir Leon Bagrit, pointed out that it was a mistake to
believe that these machines could think. There is no possibility that human beings will be controlled
by machines. Though computers are capable of learning from their mistakes and improving on their
performances, they need detailed instructions from human beings to be able to operate. They can
never lead independent lives or ‘rule the world’ by taking decisions of their own.

Sir Leon said that, in future, computers would be developed which would be small enough to
be carried in one’s pocket. Ordinary people would then be able to use them to obtain valuable
information. Computers could be plugged into a wireless network and could be used like radios. For
instance, people going on a holiday could be informed about weather conditions. Car drivers can be
given an alternative route when there is a traffic jam. It will also be possible to make tiny translating
machines. This will enable people who do not share a common language to talk to each other without
any difficulty or to read foreign publications.

It is impossible to assess the importance of a machine of this sort, for many international
misunderstandings are caused simply due to our failure to understand one another. Computers will
also be used in ordinary public hospitals. By providing a machine with a patient’s systems, a doctor
will be able to diagnose the nature of his illness. Similarly, machines could be used to keep a check on
a patient’s health record and bring it up to date. Doctors will, therefore, have immediate access to
great many facts which will help them in their work. Book-keepers and Accountants too, could be
relieved of dull clerical work. For, the tedious task of compiling and checking lists of figures could be
done entirely by machines. Computers are the most efficient servant that man has ever had, and there
is no limit to the way they can be used to improve our lives.


Questions:
(a) What is the limitation of computers? (1)
(b) In the opinion of the writer, which benefits can be derived from automation? (2)
(c) In paragraph 1, the writer says “computers can provide information in the best way”. Explain in context. (2)
(d) Is it True or False that Automation would not give any leisure time to human beings? (1)
(e) In the context of the passage, the synonym of “monotonous” is _____. (1)
(f) List two areas where computers can be used effectively. (2)
(g) How can the benefits suggested in paragraph 3 be best described? (2)
(h) Why is it fair to say that computers will help a lot even in ordinary public hospitals? (2)
(i) The writer believes that automation will bring social _____. (1)
(j) Give a suitable title for the passage. (1)
2.explanation: Answer from the passage: (a) They require detailed human instructions and cannot take independent decisions. (b) Faster accurate work and more leisure. (c) They process data to identify ways of preventing traffic accidents. (d) False. (e) Tedious / dull. (f) Hospitals and accountancy, or traffic management and translation. (g) Pocket-sized networked information and translation tools; the paragraph reference is loose, so identify the relevant benefits explicitly. (h) They aid diagnosis and keep accessible, updated patient records. (i) consequences. (j) Suggested title: Computers and Automation. The passage’s historical view of computer capabilities is reproduced for comprehension, not asserted as a current technical assessment.

1.q:
Write a précis of the following passage and supply a suitable title. (10)

The primary advantage of waking up early is that it offers a head start on the day’s tasks, The
early riser would have had finished a significant amount of work before others have gotten out of bed.
The mind is clear in the early morning, because there are few sounds or distractions, so work done at
this point is often excellent. In several instances, early risers find time for physical activity in the fresh
morning air, which provides them with energy to last until the evening. By beginning early, they ensure
that they are given sufficient time to carry out all of the work that is expected of them and are not
compelled to rush through any of it. With all of their jobs completed on time, they get a considerable
period of leisure in the evening before going to bed at the appropriate hour. They retire to bed many
hours before midnight, when sleep is most pleasant, and wakes up early the next morning in good
health and enthusiasm to face the challenges of the day.

It is obvious that such a life is far more beneficial to health than that of the person who shortens
his/her waking hours by rising late, leaving little time during the day for vital rest. Anyone who falls
asleep late must, if they desire to complete a full day’s work, work until a suitably late hour and deny
themselves the hour or two of evening exercise that they should get for their health. Despite their best
efforts, they will most likely fail to achieve the same outcomes as the early riser because they have
missed the most productive hours of the day.

It may be disputed that some people find midnight to be the absolute finest time to work. This
is undeniably true in certain situations. However, even in such instances, working late at night is not
recommended. Few people, if any, can exercise the full strength of their brain at a time when nature
prescribes sleep without jeopardising their health; and, of course, the health damage must have a
negative impact on the quality of the work done in the long term.
1.explanation: Suggested title: The Benefits of Early Rising. Summarise the author’s argument that early rising allows productive work, exercise and evening rest, while habitual late work risks health and performance. Use your own words and retain the qualification that some people find midnight productive.

3.q:
Read the passage carefully. Then choose the correct answer.

Natural disasters have become frequent occurrences in the world today. Now and again, news
of serious flooding, earthquakes and tsunamis stun us. Things are destroyed and countless lives are
lost too. When incidences such as these take place, people wonder as to the cause(s) of these
events. Could these disasters be prevented in the first place? In the race to become a developed
country and a modern society, human beings have made tremendous changes to the environment.
When humans start meddling with Mother Nature, the effects can be disastrous at times. Rapid
development has caused many problems to humans and animals alike.

Everywhere we go, it is apparent that many areas are being developed to pave the way for
modernisation. New roads, industrial areas, townships and housing areas are replacing jungles and
hilly areas. In the process, countless trees have been cut down, jungles cleared and hilly areas flattened.
It has been scientifically proven that when trees are gone, water can no longer
be contained underground. The roots of trees that act as natural defences to hold water in the ground
are no longer there to do their job. As a result, rainwater flows straight out to sea in a much shorter
time, causing frequent flash floods to places that have never faced such problems before.

Development comes at a very high price. Animals and human lives are in danger. Many land
areas are turned into housing areas, including scenic hills. Houses and apartments, some of them
very highly priced, have been built on these scenic but unsafe hills. Without careful study, and over
time, the unstable ground condition often caves in causing landslides that kill many people.

The clearing of land for all kinds of reasons has also led to the extinction of many wildlife
species. In the first place, land development causes the destruction of many animal habitats. Animals
now have to compete with humans for space and food. To survive, these animals are forced to move
deeper into the jungles. Their sources of food have become scarce, thus threatening their survival.
Smaller spaces and less food have led to the extinction of some species. Fifteen endangered animals
and six critically endangered animals in Malaysia have been identified. The Malayan Tapir, the Malayan
Tiger and the Asian elephant are three large mammal species that are on the endangered species list.
Among the critically endangered ones are the black shrew, the Malayan water shrew, the Malayan
roundleaf bat and the Sumatran rhinoceros.

It is obvious that many animals have been sacrificed in the name of development and
modernisation. Indiscriminate human activities have led to the destruction of irreplaceable and priceless
lives. There are laws to curb people from messing with our forests, polluting and doing things that can
harm our environment. There are also laws to punish those who do so, but the laws do not seem to
serve their purpose. It is the responsibility of each and every individual to preserve our fragile Earth.
If we keep destroying it, we will soon lose all that we have.

Answer the questions below based on the passage:
(a) Who are responsible for the destruction of our environment? (2)
(b) How does rainwater cause flash floods in areas where there are not many trees? (2)
(c) Give reasons why some animals have become extinct. (2)
(d) Has development brought about positive effects to our environment? Give reasons to support
your answer. (2)
(e) Who is responsible for the preservation of nature around us? (2)

2.q:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow:                                      (8×2=16)
                  Many of us believe that ‘small’ means ‘insignificant’. We believe that small actions and
       choices do not have much impact on our lives. We think that it is only the big things, the big actions
       and the big decisions that really count. But when you look at all the lives of all great people, you will
       see that they built their character through small decisions, small choices and small actions that they
       performed every day. They transformed their lives through step-by-step or day-by-day approach.
       They nurtured and nourished their good habits and chipped away their bad habits, one by one. It was
       their small day-to-day decisions that added up to make tremendous difference in the long run. Indeed,
       in matters of personal growth and character building, there is no such thing as an overnight success.
                 Growth always occurs through a sequential series of stages. There is an organic process to
       growth. When we look at children growing up, we can see this process at work: the child first learns
       to crawl, then to stand and walk and then finally to run. The same is true in the natural world. The soil
       must first be tilled and then the seed must be sown. Next, it must be nurtured with enough water and
       sunlight and only then will it grow into trees laden with ripe fruits.
                 Gandhi understood this organic process and used this universal law of nature to his benefit.
       Gandhi grew in small ways, in his day-to-day affairs. He did not wake up one day and find himself to
       be the ‘Mahatma’. In fact, there was nothing much in his early life that showed signs of greatness. But
       from his mid-twenties onwards, he deliberately and consistently attempted to change himself, reformed
       himself and grew in some small ways every day. Day by day, hour by hour, he risked failure,
       experimented and learnt from mistakes. In small as well as large situations, he took up the responsibility
       rather than avoiding it.
                This is a common factor in the lives of all great people: they exercise their freedoms and
       choices in small ways that make great impact on their lives and their environment. Each of their small
       decisions and actions, add up to have a profound impact in the long run. By understanding this
       principle, we can move forward, with confidence, in the direction of our dreams. Often when our
       ideal goal, looks too far from us, we become easily discouraged, disheartened and pessimistic.


     However, when we choose to grow in small ways, by taking small steps one at a time, our achievement
     becomes easy.


  (i) The main idea in the first paragraph is that :
       (a) big things, big actions and big decisions make a person great.
       (b) small actions and decisions are important in one’s life.
       (c) overnight success is possible for all of us.
       (d) personal changes are not important.
 (ii) What does the writer mean by saying ‘chipped away at their bad habits’?
       (a) Steadily gave up bad habits.                (b) Slowly produced bad habits.
       (c) Gradually criticized bad habits.            (d) Did not like bad habits.
 (iii) What is done by great people to transform their lives?
        (a) They approach life on a day-to-day basis.      (b) They build character in small ways.
        (c) They believe in performing every day.          (d) All of these.
 (iv) How can we grow in small ways?
       (a) By getting disheartened.                        (b) By dreaming little.
       (c) By taking small steps one at a time.            (d) None of these.
 (v) How did Gandhiji become ‘Mahatma’?
      (a) By risking failures.                             (b) By learning from mistakes.
      (c) By taking up responsibilities.                   (d) All of the above.
 (vi) What according to the author is the universal law of nature?
       (a) Everything takes time to grow.                  (b) Nothing can change in a day.
       (c) Both (a) & (b)                                  (d) Neither (a) nor (b)
(vii) Pick out the word/phrase which is similar in meaning to ‘purposely’
       (a) intentionally                                  (b) deliberately
       (c) in small ways                                  (d) consistently
(viii) Pick the right option in which the word ‘Principle’ has been used in the same way as in Para 4 of the
       passage
        (a) He was a man of principle and good to his word.
        (b) The ambassador refused on principle to agree to the terms of the accord.
        (c) By one count, rice is the principle source of calories for about half the planet.
        (d) Wilson constructed various forms of electric wave detector depending on this same principle.
                                                   -3-
2.explanation: Passage answers: (i) B—small actions and decisions matter; (ii) A—steadily gave up bad habits; (iii) D—all of these; (iv) C—small steps; (v) D—all of the above. (vi) A expresses gradual growth; C is probably intended but B’s absolute “nothing can change in a day” is too sweeping. (vii) Deliberately is the word used in the passage; intentionally is also synonymous with purposely, so without a passage-word restriction A and B overlap. (viii) D uses principle as an underlying rule rather than a moral conviction. C misprints principal as principle. These are guidance for the conventional response sheet, not machine-scored subquestions.

2.q: Write a précis of the following passage in about 1/3 of its original length, giving it suitable title.(10) Trees give shade for the benefit of others, and while they themselves must stand directly in the sun and endure the scorching heat of the day, they continue to produce the fruit by which others profit. They do not hoard their gifts, nor do they complain of the weather. The character of good and noble men is exactly like that of these trees. We must ask ourselves: what is the use of this perishable body, which is destined to decay, if no use of it is made for the lasting benefit of mankind? A life lived only for the self is a life wasted. Consider the natural world and the lessons it yields. Take sandalwood- the more it is rubbed against a hard surface, the more of its sweet scent does it yield to the air. Consider the sugarcane— the more it is peeled, crushed, and cut into small pieces, the more delicious juice does it produce for the thirsty. Look at gold—the more it is burnt in the crucible of the forge, the more brightly and purely does it shine. The men who are truly noble at heart do not lose these divine qualities even in the process of losing their very lives. To them, the external world is secondary. What does it matter whether common men praise them or not? What difference does it make whether great riches abide with them or whether they live in poverty? What does it signify whether they die at this very moment or whether their lives are prolonged for many years? Happen what may, those who tread in the right path of righteousness will not set foot in any other, for their integrity is absolute. Life itself is unprofitable and hollow to a man who does not live for the service of others. To live for the mere sake of living one’s own life is to live the base life of dogs and cows, driven only by instinct. Those who lay down their lives, even for the sake of a friend, or even for the sake of a complete stranger, will assuredly dwell forever in a world of eternal bliss.
2.explanation: Suggested title: A Life of Service. Summarise how the author uses trees, sandalwood, sugarcane and gold as images of selfless service and integrity through hardship. Retain the argument that honour, wealth and lifespan matter less than benefiting others. Write about one third of the passage in your own words.

4.q:
Read the following passage and answer the question given below: Many people believe that science and religion are contrary to each other. But this notion is wrong. As a matter of fact, both are complementary to each other. The aim of both these institutions is to explain different aspects of life, universe and human existence. There is no doubt that the methods of science and religion are different. The method of science is observation, experimentation and experience. Science takes its recourse to progressive march towards perfection; the rules of religion are faith, intuition and spoken word of the enlightened; in general, while science is inclined towards reason and rationality, spiritualism is the essence of religion. In earlier times when man appeared on earth, he was over-awed at the sight of violent and powerful aspects of nature. In certain cases, the usefulness of different natural objects of nature overwhelmed man. Thus began the worship of forces of nature-fire, the sun, the rivers, the rocks, the trees, the snakes, etc. The holy scriptures were written by those who had developed harmony between external nature and their inner self. Their object was to ennoble, elevate and liberate the human spirit and mind. But the priestly class took upon itself the monopoly of scriptural knowledge and interpretation to its own advantage. Thus the entire human race was in chains. Truth was flouted and progressive, liberal and truthful ideas or ideas expressing doubt and skepticism were suppressed and their holders punished. It was in these trying circumstances, the science emerged as a saviour of mankind. But its path was not smooth and safe. The scientists and free thinkers were tortured. This was the fate of Copernicus, Galileo, Bruno and others. But by and by science gain ground.
(a) Why does man worship the force of nature? (2)
(b) Why does the passage say that science emerged as a saviour of mankind? (2)
(c) How does it distinguish science’s methods from religion’s? (2)
(d) What treatment did early scientists like Galileo and Bruno face, and why? (2)
(e) How does the author argue against science and religion being contrary? (2)
4.explanation: According to the passage: (a) Awe at powerful natural forces and appreciation of useful natural objects led to worship. (b) Science challenged suppression of truth and free inquiry. (c) Science uses observation, experimentation and experience; religion uses faith, intuition and teachings of the enlightened. (d) Early thinkers were tortured or persecuted for challenging established interpretations. (e) The author argues that both explain aspects of life and existence through different, complementary methods. These are comprehension answers representing the author’s claims.

1.q:
Write a precis of the passage given below: (10)

Culture is a forbidding word. I have to use it, knowing of none better to describe the various
beautiful and interesting objects which man has made in the past and handed down to us, and which
some of us are hoping to hand on. Many people despise them. They argue with force that cultural
stuff takes up a great deal of room and time, and better be scrapped.

Cultivated people are like drops in an ocean. They mix easily and genially with other drops, for
those exclusive days are over when cultivated people made only cultivated friends, and became
tongue-tied or terror-struck in the presence of anyone whose make-up was different from their own.
Culture, thank goodness, is no longer a social asset, it can no longer be employed either as a barrier
against the mob or as a ladder into the aristocracy.

All the same, we are a drop in the ocean. Few people share our enjoyment so far. Strictly
between ourselves, and keeping our limited circulation in mind, let us put our heads together and
consider for a moment our special problem, our special blessings, our special woes. No one needs to
listen to us who does not want to. We whisper in the corner of a world which is full of others’ noises,
and louder ones.

Come closer, our problem, as I see it, is what we have got worth passing on. What we have is
(roughly speaking) a little knowledge about books, pictures, tunes, and a little skill in their interpretation.
Seated beside our gas fires, and beneath our electric bulbs, we inherit a tradition that has lasted for
about three thousand years.
1.explanation: Suggested title: Preserving Cultural Inheritance. Summarise culture as inherited achievements in books, art and music; the small number who appreciate it; its loss of use as a social-status barrier; and the responsibility to pass knowledge and interpretation to later generations. Do not add external cultural criticism.

3.q:
Read the given passage carefully and answer the questions that follow.

A majority taken collectively may be regarded as a being whose opinions and, most frequently,
whose interests are opposed to those of another being, which is styled a minority. If it is admitted that
a man possessing absolute power may misuse that power by wronging his adversaries, why should a
majority not be liable to the same reproach? Men are not apt to change their characters by
agglomeration; nor does their patience in the presence of obstacles increase with the consciousness
of their strength. For these reasons we should not willingly invest any group of our fellows with that

unlimited authority which we should refuse to any individual.



One social power must always predominate over others, but liberty is endangered when this
power is checked by no obstacles which may retard its course and force it to moderate its own
vehemence. Unlimited power is in itself a bad and dangerous thing, and no power on earth is so
worthy of honor for itself or of reverential obedience to the rights which it represents that we should
admit its uncontrolled and all-predominant authority. When the right and means of absolute command
are conferred on a people or a king, on an aristocracy or a democracy, a monarchy or a republic,
there has been implanted the germ of tyranny.

The main evil of the present democratic institutions of the United States does not arise, as is
often asserted in Europe, from their weakness, but from their overpowering strength; the excessive
liberty which reigns in that country is not so alarming as is the very inadequate security which exists
against tyranny.

When an individual or a party is wronged in the United States, to whom can he apply for
redress? If to the public opinion, public opinion constitutes the majority; if to the legislature, it represents
the majority and implicitly obeys its injunctions; if to the executive power, it is appointed by the
majority and remains a passive tool in its hands; the public troops consist of the majority under arms;
the jury is the majority invested with the right of hearing judicial cases, and in certain states even the
judges are elected by the majority. However iniquitous or absurd the evil complained about, no sure
barrier is established to defend against it.


Find the passage words matching: (a) autocracy [freedom/tyranny/liberty/anarchy]; (b) opponents [leaders/partners/adversaries/allies]; (c) blame [reproach/praise/reward/ignore]; (d) collection [dispersion/agglomeration/separation/scattering]; (e) nobility [aristocracy/democracy/oligarchy/monarchy]; (f) wicked [virtuous/justified/iniquitous/benign]. (6×1=6)
(g) What is the main theme of the passage? (3)
(h) What is the author’s main concern regarding unlimited power? (3)
(i) What is the author’s argument about individual liberty? (3)
3.explanation: Vocabulary answers: tyranny; adversaries; reproach; agglomeration; aristocracy; iniquitous. (g) The passage warns against unchecked majority power. (h) Unlimited authority can become tyranny whether held by one person or a group. (i) Liberty needs effective checks and avenues of redress against the dominant power. Answer according to the historical author’s argument, rather than treating it as a current assessment of US institutions.

2.q:
Write a précis of the following passage in about a third of its length: (15)
A majority of Indians prefer to use the internet for accessing banking and other financial services
than shopping online, shows a new survey.

Almost 57% of Indian respondents using the internet prefer to bank online and use other financial
services due to hassel-free access and time saving feature of online banking according to the survey.

Checking information on products and services online comes a close second at 53% while
50% shop for products online. The fourth on the list - around 42% of respondents in India surfed
online to look for jobs, the survey said. Online banking has made things much easier for the people
and it saves a lot of time.

It has eliminated the problems associated with traditional way of banking where one has to
stand in a queue and fill up several forms. Most of the banks in India have introduced customer-
friendly online banking facility with advanced security features to protect customers against cybercrime.

The easy registration process for net banking has improved customers’ access to several banking
products increased customer loyalty, facilitated money transfer to any bank across India and has help
banks-attract new customers. The Indian results closely track the global trends as well conducted
among 19216 people from 24 countries, the survey showed that banking and keeping track of finances
and searching for jobs are the main tasks of internet users around the globe.

Overall, 60% of people surveyed used the web to check their bank account and other financial
assets in the past 90 days, making it the most popular use of the internet globally. Shopping was not
too far behind at 48%, the survey showed and 41% went online in search of a job in terms of country
preferences, almost 90% of respondents in Sweden use e-banking.

Online banking has also caught on in a big way in nations like France, Canada, Australia,
Poland, South Africa and Belgium, the survey showed. The Germans and British come on top for
using online shopping with 74% of respondents in both countries having bought something online in
the past three months. They are followed by 68% of respondents in Sweden, 65% in US and 62% in
South Korea.

1.q:
Write a précis of the following passage. (14) Exploration and quarrying operations in the North-Eastern hill regions, particularly in states like Mizoram, encounter unique structural and environmental vulnerabilities that distinguish them from mining activities in mainland Indian plateaus. The combination of steep terrain, high-intensity monsoon rainfall, and young, seismically active geological formations creates a high-risk environment for standard extraction methods. Minor minerals, primarily sandstone and stone boulders used for regional infrastructure, are frequently extracted through small-scale, fragmented quarrying units.

Unfortunately, these units often lack the engineering capacity to manage high vertical faces, leading to frequent slope failures and landslides that endanger both labour and nearby settlements. Furthermore, the practice of stone crushing near highway corridors generates significant particulate matter, which degrades air quality and settles on surrounding vegetation, causing long-term agricultural distress.

To mitigate these localized hazards, mining administrative bodies must mandate systematic terracing and bench-formation protocols tailored specifically to steep slopes. It is no longer sufficient to regulate mineral revenue alone; the administration must actively oversee the hydrological impact of quarrying. Proper drainage networks must be constructed around lease areas to prevent rainwater accumulation from liquefying the soil overburden. Furthermore, the District Mineral Foundation (DMF) funds must be strategically utilized to rehabilitate abandoned quarry sites through targeted afforestation and loose-boulder check dams. Balancing the accelerating demand for construction aggregates with the ecological preservation of fragile hill slopes represents the defining administrative challenge for modern mining controllers in the region.

While Mizoram is not characterized by large-scale heavy metalliferous deposits like the iron or coal belts of central India, its unique inventory of non-metallic resources, including high-grade sandstone, shale, and potential clay deposits, forms the backbone of its localized industrial growth. The strategic position of the state, serving as a gateway for trans-national infrastructure projects like the Kaladan Multi-Modal Transit Transport Project, has exponentially escalated the domestic consumption of these structural minerals.

However, translating this resource wealth into equitable economic development requires a departure from ad-hoc extraction practices. The state’s mineral policy must prioritize structured resource appraisal over hasty extraction to ensure long-term availability. Unregulated quarrying not only causes revenue leakage through illegal transport networks but also prevents the state from commanding fair market value for its natural assets.

To rectify this, the modern mining administration must deploy digital monitoring tools, such as drone-based volumetric surveys and electronic transit passes, to plug leakage and accurately map the depletion rates of active stone quarries. Simultaneously, economic growth must not alienate local communities. Under the current mineral governance paradigms, sustainable development requires that a portion of the royalties collected be re-invested into local village councils for infrastructure and health initiatives. By transitioning from a primitive, revenue-only collection mindset to an asset-management approach, the state can secure its infrastructural self-reliance without bankrupting its environmental capital. The objective is to establish a system where mineral extraction funds long-term regional development rather than short-term private gain.

3.q:
Read the following passage and answer the questions that follow:
 The mining and processing of minerals provides us with the building blocks required to form much of the infrastructure needed to support modern societies. However, the process of mining remains intense and invasive, and operations often leave environmental impacts on the local surroundings as well as wider implications for the environmental health of the planet.

Mining and mineral processing operations often have high water footprints as many stages require the use of water. Examples include dust mitigation, removing soluble particles, sieving and separation processes, and in creating tailings dams for waste management. High water use in mining operations can lead to reduced access for local people to uncontaminated freshwater supplies and can result in a local area suffering from water stress. However, compared to other industries, mining has a relatively small water usage and often a large fraction of the water used is saline so it does not have much use in other industries or domestically.

Another issue related to environmental pollution caused by mining is that of leakages of mining tailings. Mining tailings are the materials left behind after the economically valuable fraction of material has been extracted. Modern mining programmes often aim to remove these harmful but valuable chemicals to reuse for further mineral separation. In addition to improving efficiency and cutting costs, this minimises the risk of environmental damage by reducing the toxicity of the tailings.

Overall, when considering the environmental ramifications of mining, it is important to weigh up the social and environmental damages caused by extracting the minerals against the benefits gained from the use of the final product. Mining of further resources is required to support the growing global population, but it should allow for the creation of green infrastructure and renewable energy generation. It is vital that governments and companies continue to innovate to create clean mining technologies with strict environmental regulations which will enable the mining industry to pave the way for a sustainable and hopeful future. 
1. What are the ways in which water is used in mining?(2) 
2. How can environmental damage from mining tailings be reduced?(2) 
3. What can governments and companies do to mitigate the environmental damages caused by mining? (2)

1.q: Write a précis of the following passage : (14) Economic inequality is a persistent and growing issue that affects societies worldwide. It refers to the unequal distribution of income, wealth, and opportunities among individuals and groups. While some level of inequality is inevitable in any society, excessive economic disparity can lead to social unrest, reduced economic mobility, and weakened social cohesion. One of the primary drivers of economic inequality is the disparity in education and skills. Individuals with higher levels of education and specialised skills tend to have better job prospects and higher incomes. In contrast, those with limited education and skills often face difficulties in securing well-paying jobs, leading to a widening income gap. This educational inequality is often rooted in socio-economic factors, such as access to quality schools, parental support, and community resources. The labour market also plays a significant role in economic inequality. Technological advancements and globalization have created high-demand, high-paying jobs in certain sectors, while other sectors experience job losses and wage stagnation. This has resulted in a polarized labour market, where a small proportion of workers enjoy significant financial rewards, while many others struggle to make ends meet. Additionally, factors such as gender, race, and ethnicity can further exacerbate labour market inequalities, leading to systemic discrimination and biases. Wealth inequality is another critical aspect of economic disparity. Wealth, which includes assets such as property, investments, and savings, tends to be highly concentrated among a small proportion of the population. This concentration of wealth allows the affluent to generate more income through investments and access better opportunities, perpetuating a cycle of inequality. Conversely, those with little or no wealth have limited financial security and opportunities for upward mobility. Addressing economic inequality requires comprehensive policy interventions. Governments can play a pivotal by implementing progressive taxation, investing in education and skills development, and promoting social safety nets. Progressive taxation ensures that those with higher incomes contribute a fair share to public resources, while investments in education can help bridge the skills gap and provide equal opportunities for all. Social safety nets, such as unemployment benefits and healthcare, can provide financial security and support for those in need. In conclusion, economic inequality is a complex and multifaceted issue that poses significant challenges to social and economic stability. By addressing the root causes of inequality and implementing inclusive policies, we can work towards a more equitable society where all individuals have the opportunity to thrive and contribute to economic growth.

3.q:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow : There is absolutely no point in complaining that over the years, there has been pressure for increased productivity and higher earnings for workers in industry. There are several ways for increasing employees earnings. Employee earnings can be increased by raising the selling price of the firm’s products and services, reducing profits or costs of raw materials, or augmenting labour productivity. However, increasing employee earning by means other than increased labour productivity jeopardizes the firm’s competitive strength in the market. Higher prices usually mean fewer customer, reduced profit means less capital investment, and low-cost material mean poor product quality. But, increasing labour productivity by enhancing skills and motivation creates an almost unlimited resource. The development of economic resources, human as well as nonhuman, is the product of human effort, and the quality of human effort in large part depends on human motivation.

Enthusing employees with workaholic spirit through traditional authority and financial incentives has become increasingly difficult as employees become economically secure and their dependency on any one particular organization decreases. According to expectancy theorists, the motivation to work increases when an employee feels his performance is an instrument for obtaining desired rewards. Nevertheless, in many organization today employees are entitled to organizational rewards just by being employed. Unions, governmental regulations, and the nature of the job itself in some cases prevent management from relating financial rewards to performance. People may be attracted to join and remain in organizations to receive organizational rewards, but being motivated to join an organization is not the same as being motivated to exert effort in an organization. The challenge to management is to find and administer alternative form of incentives which will induce employees to improve work performance. The Coliseum is an ancient stadium in the center of Rome. It is the largest of its kind. They
started building it in the year 70. It took ten years to build it. The Coliseum has been used in many

opts.b: The sensational nature of the festival

25.passage:
As the sun climbs in the cloudless sky, visitors are rewarded with their first glimpse of Dakhla
refugee camp in western Algeria. It isn’t the most obvious setting for a film festival, but for seven
years, just before the glitz and glamour of Cannes, the Sahrawi people of Dakhla have hosted actors
and film makers from around the world for this six day event. This year, for the first time direct flights
were laid on from London, giving the opportunity for overseas visitors to play a part in this
extraordinary occasion. But despite the energy and excitement, the background to the film festival is a
serious one, as the Sahrawi people have been living for thirty years in this isolated desert outpost,
having been forced to flee their native Western Sahara. Western Africa, Africas last colony, was taken
over by Morocco when the Spanish withdrew in 1976, despite a ruling from the International Court of
Justice. This was followed by a brutal 16 year war, during which time tens of thousands of Sahrawis
fled across the Algerian border to refugee camp. In 1991, a ceasefire, a referendum on self determination
was promised to decide the fate of the country and its people. However, almost twenty years later, the
gears of diplomacy have turned slowly and nothing has happened. Meanwhile the refugees have been
left- stranded in five refugee camps dotted around the vast inhospitable desert. Of these, Dakhla is the
most remote and unlike its namesake, the beautiful coastal city in western Sahara, this Dakhla has no
paved roads and is entirely dependent on outside supplies for food and water.

17.passage:
It is strange that,according to his position in life,an extravagant man is admired or despised.A successful
businessman does nothing to increase his popularity by being careful with his money. He is expected to
display his success, to have a smart car, an expensive life, and to be lavish with his hospitality. If he is not
so, he is considered mean and his reputation in business may even suffer in consequence. The paradox
remains that if he had not been careful with his money in the first place, he would never have achieved his
present wealth. Among the low income groups,a different set of values exists.The young clerk who makes
his wife a present of a new dress when he hadn’t paid his house rent, is condemned as extravagant.Carefulness
with money to the point of meanness is applauded as a virtue.Nothing in his life is considered more worthy
than paying his bills.The ideal wife for such a man separates her housekeeping money into joyless little piles
–so much for rent, for food, for the children’s shoes; she is able to face the milkman with equanimity and
never knows the guilt of buying something she can’t really afford. As for myself, I fall into neither of these
categories. If I have money to spare, I can be extravagant, but when, as is usually the case, I am hard up,
then I am the meanest man imaginable.

1.q: Write an essay in about 500 words on why we should protect our environment. (25)
1.explanation: A strong essay can explain ecological and human reasons for protecting the environment, then organize practical measures at individual, community and government levels. Use concrete examples such as forests, water, pollution, biodiversity and climate, and conclude with shared responsibility.
1.sourceNote: Independent writing guidance, not an official model answer.

2.q: Write a précis on the following passage. (25)
2.explanation: Identify the passage’s central argument: persistent illiteracy is a distinct development problem and can contribute to high birth rates; eliminating it needs targeted access through primary schools, part-time centres and adult functional-literacy programmes. A précis should retain the thesis and main proposed measures, omit examples/repetition, use concise wording and add a suitable title.
2.sourceNote: Independent writing guidance, not an official model answer.

1.q: It is difficult to sustain proper health devoid of
1.passage:
Good health depends on several things. Fresh air and sunlight are very important for our health. Fresh air helps us to improve our immune system and overall health. So a morning walk is very useful for health. Sunlight helps our body to produce vitamin-D. A dirty and damp atmosphere causes lots of diseases. Fresh and pure drinking water is also necessary for good health. Impure drinking- water is the cause of several diseases. So, we must take care of these things. Food is another necessary thing for the body. Nutritious foods help us to maintain good health. Consumption of healthy foods helps us to minimize any health related problems. We all should know, how, when and what to eat. We should always include a portion of green vegetables, fruits or salads in our meal. Green vegetables are sources of vital nutrients. Our digestive system plays a key role in our overall health. Fiber rich foods such as whole grain wheat, bran rice, etc. help us improve our digestive system. A balanced and nutritious diet helps the proper growth of the body. But we must remember that we eat to live and not that we live to eat. In India, over-eating causes a large number of deaths. If we eat less, we may live more.

Cleanliness is essential for good health. Without cleanliness, it is very difficult to maintain proper health. We should clear our house and the surrounding areas every day. Every day, we should bath twice, in the morning and in the evening. After eating food, we should clean our hands with soap.

Various types of diseases erupt from unclean surroundings. We should always throw the garbage in the dustbin. A disease-free body is a healthy body, and cleanliness is the key for health. We must know some simple rules of hygiene. Our house must be airy and sunny. Apart from all this, we must form good habits. We should keep ourselves free from cares and anxieties. Early rising is equally necessary for good health. So we must try to keep fit. Health is the real wealth. Health is a great treasure. It is the highest blessing. It is the source of all happiness. Money can’t buy happiness. Happiness is priceless and not dependent upon the wealth of a person. Good health, however, contribute to the emotional well-being and happiness of a person. Even with limited income, a person with sound health can lead a happy and enjoyable life.

1.explanation: The printed passage (pages 1–2) states, “Cleanliness is essential for good health. Without cleanliness, it is very difficult to maintain proper health.” Health therefore cannot be sustained without cleanliness, so the choice is (b) Cleanliness.

2.explanation: The printed passage (pages 1–2) states, “Impure drinking- water is the cause of several diseases.” Water that is not clean and pure therefore leads to several diseases — (a).

3.explanation: The printed passage (pages 1–2) states, “Nutritious foods help us to maintain good health,” and “We should always include a portion of green vegetables, fruits or salads in our meal.” The food we should constantly try to eat is therefore nutritious — (c).

4.explanation: The printed passage (pages 1–2) states, “Happiness is priceless and not dependent upon the wealth of a person.” Happiness is the thing that does not depend on wealth — (b).

5.explanation: The printed passage (pages 1–2) states, “Good health depends on several things. Fresh air and sunlight are very important for our health,” together with “a portion of green vegetables, fruits or salads” and “A balanced and nutritious diet helps the proper growth of the body.” Fresh air, green vegetables and a proper diet are all named, so (d) All of these.

6.explanation: The printed passage (pages 1–2) states, “Health is the real wealth. Health is a great treasure. It is the highest blessing. It is the source of all happiness,” and, in the next sentence, “Money can’t buy happiness.” The source of all happiness is therefore (d) Health.

7.explanation: The printed passage (pages 1–2) states, “Apart from all this, we must form good habits.” One must cultivate good (b) habits to stay healthy.

8.explanation: The printed passage (pages 1–2) states, “Good health, however, contribute to the emotional well-being and happiness of a person.” Emotional well-being is contributed to by (a) Good health.

9.explanation: The printed passage (pages 1–2) states, “We should keep ourselves free from cares and anxieties.” The thing to be kept free from is (a) Anxieties.

10.explanation: The printed passage (pages 1–2) states, “Our house must be airy and sunny.” Airy and sunny are therefore the ideal conditions for a house — (b). The other printed choices describe what the passage calls unhealthy: “A dirty and damp atmosphere causes lots of diseases.”

11.explanation: The printed passage (pages 1–2) states, “A balanced and nutritious diet helps the proper growth of the body.” The factor that contributes to proper growth is therefore (d) Balanced and nutritious diet.

12.explanation: The printed passage (pages 1–2) states, “After eating food, we should clean our hands with soap.” The way to keep clean after a meal is (a) Clean our hands with soap.

13.explanation: A sweeping statement is a broad, indiscriminate generalisation that ignores particular cases; it is made without due thought about its exceptions. None of the printed choices states that standard sense exactly: “Wonderful statement” is positive, “Meaningless statement” claims the statement has no meaning at all, and “Inconsistent statement” claims it contradicts itself or other statements. The only printed choice that fits how a sweeping statement is produced is (d) Thoughtless statement, so (d) is the best of the four. Confidence is medium because the standard sense (“over-generalised”) is missing from the printed option set.

14.explanation: “To have a green thumb” is the idiom for having a natural interest or talent, especially with plants; the other printed colours are not idioms here. The answer is (b) Green Thumb.

15.explanation: “A white elephant” is the idiom for a costly or troublesome possession that costs more than it is worth; a white cat, white leopard and white owl are not. The answer is (c) A white elephant.

16.explanation: “To take to one’s heels” means to run away in fear; the printed option (a) Took to heels expresses this. “Took off” means departed, “took a jet” is literal, and “took away” means removed — (a).

17.explanation: The “green-eyed monster” is the traditional idiom for jealousy; the other eye-colour options are not idioms. The answer is (a) Green-eyed monster.

18.explanation: “To spill the beans” means to reveal information indiscreetly; spilling milk, tea or water is literal only. The answer is (b) Spilling the beans.

19.explanation: “To have an axe to grind” means to have a private interest or motive to serve; “bury the hatchet” means end a quarrel, “went to the winds” means disappeared and “at one’s wit’s end” means baffled. The answer is (c) An axe to grind.

20.explanation: “To shake in one’s shoes” means to tremble with fear; “fits and starts” describes irregular effort, “close shave” a narrow escape and “bad blood” hostility. The answer is (d) Shake in shoes.

21.explanation: “To sow wild oats” means to indulge in irresponsible pleasure-seeking while young; the other printed options mean approaching a limit, rising from ashes and an unavoidable choice. The answer is (b) Sowing wild oats.

22.explanation: “A bolt from the blue” is something unexpected and unpleasant arriving without warning; a red letter day is a happy occasion, “burn one’s boat” means burn one’s options and a sore point is an irritant. The answer is (d) A bolt from the blue.

23.explanation: “To have the last laugh” means to be victorious at the end of an argument or dispute; “throw down a glove” challenges, “turn a deaf ear” ignores and “steer clear of” avoids. The answer is (c) Have the last laugh.

24.explanation: “A damp squib” is something that fizzles out and fails — a disappointing result; “in cold blood” means ruthlessly, “smell a rat” means suspect treachery and “give vent to” means express. The answer is (a) A damp squib.

25.explanation: “To be in the same boat” (printed as “Sailing in the same boat”) means to be in the same difficult situation as someone else; the other options mean losing position, causing anger and making matters worse. The answer is (b) Sailing in the same boat.

26.explanation: “The gift of the gab” is the ability to speak well and fluently; “hand in glove” means close cooperation, “soft option” the easier course and “speak one’s mind” say what one thinks. The answer is (d) Gift of the gab.

27.explanation: The “carrot and stick” policy is the combined use of reward (carrot) and punishment (stick); “ins and outs” are details, “eat everyone’s salt” means live on others and “hand in glove” means in close alliance. The answer is (a) Carrot and stick.

28.explanation: “To toe the line” means to follow the lead by conforming to the expected standard; “stick to guns” means persist, “null and void” means invalid and “leaps and bounds” means rapidly. The answer is (b) To toe the line.

29.explanation: The underlined word “went” is the past tense of “go” and is the finite verb of the sentence, so it is a verb — (b).

30.explanation: The underlined word “heavy” qualifies the noun “load” by describing it, so it is an adjective — (c).

31.explanation: The underlined word “critically” modifies the verb “evaluated” by telling how the information was evaluated, so it is an adverb — (d).

32.explanation: The printed page (page 4) underlines “about” in “Brian often talked about Ms. Rita.” “About” introduces the object of “talked”, so it is a preposition — (a). A differently transcribed legacy copy of this sentence names “often” as the underlined word and therefore answers “Adverb”; on this printed paper the underline is on “about”, and “often” (an adverb of frequency) is not underlined here, so the derived answer follows the print.

33.explanation: The underlined word “his” is the possessive form standing for a person’s; among the printed choices (Noun, Verb, Pronoun, Conjunction) it is a pronoun — (c).

34.explanation: The underlined word “yet” joins the two clauses “He was not handsome” and “he was a successful actor” as a contrasting coordinating conjunction, so it is a conjunction — (b).

35.explanation: The underlined word “justice” names an idea or quality that cannot be seen or touched, so it is an abstract noun — (a).

36.explanation: The underlined word “seldom” answers how often Dr. Clancy is wrong, so it is an adverb of frequency — (c), not of manner, time or degree.

37.explanation: The underlined word “much” in “feeling much better” measures how great the improvement is, so it is an adverb of degree — (d).

38.explanation: The auxiliary “have” needs a past participle: “I have already eaten.” “already ate” and “had ate” are not past participles, and “have had eaten” is ungrammatical, so (b) already eaten.

39.explanation: The gerund “Travelling” is a singular subject, so it takes “has become”; the present perfect suits a change completed in the twentieth century and holding now. “have become” disagrees in number, “had became” is not a past participle, and the past perfect “had become” has no past reference point in the sentence. The answer is (c) has become.

40.explanation: “Mark and I” is a compound (plural) subject, and “since Kindergarten” calls for the present perfect: “have known each other”. “has known” and “has knew” disagree in number and “had knew” is not a past participle. The answer is (b) have known.

41.explanation: “Police” is a plural noun (a body of officers), so it takes the plural verb “were”; “would not able” lacks a verb form and “was/is not able” disagree in number. The answer is (a) were not able.

43.explanation: Children climb on the monkey bars — the structure is climbed over and across, not entered: “into” needs an enclosed space, “in” does not express climbing up onto the frame, and “to” only indicates direction. The answer is (a) on.

46.explanation: The adverb must fit the scene: a boy looking at a box of chocolate. “Greedily” is the choice the item is built around — chocolate provokes desire — and it is the most characteristic description of the look. “Happily”, “angrily” and “carelessly” are grammatical but need a context the stem does not supply, so with chocolate as the cue the best of the four printed options is (d) greedily. Confidence is medium because no context in the print rules the others out.

47.explanation: The table lies between exactly two chairs; “among” requires three or more, “besides” means “in addition to”, and “within” means inside. The answer is (c) between.

48.explanation: The printed line is the proverb “Make hay while the sun shines” (printed “May hay _________ the sun shines”), which means use the opportunity while it lasts; the proverb requires “while”. The answer is (d) while. (“May hay” is a printed misprint for “Make hay”, preserved as printed.)

49.explanation: “Bob and Ronny ate too much and felt sick” contains one independent clause with a compound subject (Bob and Ronny) and a compound predicate (ate … and felt sick). A sentence with a single clause stays simple even when its subject and predicate are compound; a compound sentence would need two independent clauses, and there is no subordinate clause either. The answer is (c) Simple Sentence.

50.explanation: “I spoke to your friend in English” and “he responded in Mizo” are two independent clauses joined by the coordinating conjunction “but”, with no subordinate clause, so the sentence is compound — (b).

51.explanation: The independent clause “Lucy returned the computer” is followed by the subordinate clause “after she knew it was damaged”, so the sentence has one independent and one dependent clause: complex — (a).

52.explanation: The sentence has two independent clauses — “My parents usually go for a walk” and “it was raining today” — joined by “but”, plus the subordinate clause “while the sun sets”. Two independents plus one subordinate clause give compound-complex — (d).

53.explanation: “Only God can help us” is a positive statement: no negation, no question, no command. It is therefore an affirmative sentence — (a).

54.explanation: The sentence carries the negation “doesn’t” (does not), which is the feature the item tests. “Assertive” is the broader class that includes affirmative sentences as well, so the specific and correct printed label here is (c) Negative Sentence.

55.explanation: “Who doesn’t wish to be happy?” is a wh-question ending in a question mark, so its sentence type is interrogative — (b). The “doesn’t” belongs to the question form and does not turn it into a plain negative statement.

56.explanation: “did not” negates the verb, so the sentence is negative — (c). As in Q54, “Assertive” is the wider class (statements), while the distinguishing printed feature here is the negation.

57.explanation: “Hurrah!” expresses a sudden joyful feeling, so the sentence is exclamatory — (a). It is neither a question, a negation nor a plain statement.

58.explanation: “Let us go out for a walk” expresses a request or suggestion with the verb in its base form and no stated subject, which is the imperative mood — (c).

60.explanation: The two printed sentences contrast: having a lot of money on one side, being very unhappy on the other. Option (b) keeps both facts and marks the contrast with “In spite of”. Option (a) is ungrammatical (“has a lot of money and unhappy too”), while (c) and (d) replace the printed contrast with a false cause of the unhappiness. The answer is (b) In spite of having a lot of money my neighbour is very unhappy.

65.explanation: An anarchist is a person who believes the state should be abolished and advocates a state of lawlessness; an atheist denies God, an amateur is a non-professional and an arsonist sets fires. The answer is (c) Anarchist.

66.explanation: A connoisseur is a critical judge of any art or craft; a cacographer writes badly, a cynosure is the centre of attention and a coquette is a flirting woman. The answer is (a) Connoisseur.

67.explanation: A congregation is a group of people gathered for worship; a constellation is a group of stars, crusaders are campaigners and a curator tends a museum collection. The answer is (c) Congregation.

68.explanation: A crèche (printed “Creche”) is a nursery for babies and young children; crochet is a form of needlework, cricket a sport and croquet a lawn game. The answer is (d) Creche.

69.explanation: The combining form “biblio-” means book, so fear of books is bibliophobia; bathophobia is fear of depths, dipsophobia fear of drinking and “Geraphobia” is not the term for books. The answer is (d) Bibliophobia.

70.explanation: Ephemeral means lasting a very short time; eternal and everlasting mean lasting for ever, and eternity is a noun for infinite time. The answer is (a) Ephemeral.

71.explanation: Indelible marks or ink cannot be removed or erased; incredible means unbelievable, inedible means not fit to eat and impossible means not possible. The answer is (b) Indelible.

72.explanation: A cynic sneers at the aims and beliefs of other people; a misogynist hates women, a linguist studies language and a sceptic doubts. The answer is (a) Cynic.

73.explanation: The verb “absorbed” takes the preposition “in”: “absorbed in his work”. The other printed prepositions do not complete the collocation. The answer is (a) absorbed in.

74.explanation: The adjective “angry” takes “with” before a person: “angry with him”. The answer is (d) angry with.

75.explanation: The verb “conform” is followed by “to”: “conform to the rules”. The answer is (b) conform to.

76.explanation: The fixed collocation is “an exception to the rule”; the other printed prepositions are not used with “exception” in this sense. The answer is (c) exception to.

77.explanation: “Leave for” a place means to depart towards it: “They are leaving for India soon.” The answer is (b) leaving for.

78.explanation: “Capable” takes “of” followed by a gerund: “capable of doing that”. The answer is (c) of doing.

79.explanation: After the auxiliary “did” the main verb must be the bare form: “Did you go to school yesterday?” “went” would repeat the past marking, “leave” does not fit “to school” here and “going” is not a bare infinitive. The answer is (d) go.

80.explanation: “As if” introduces a comparison that is not real: Ruth does not actually know everything, so English uses the simple past subjunctive — “as if she knew everything”. “knows”, “know” and “known” do not give the unreal comparison tested here. The answer is (a) knew.

30.explanation: “such” points out the kind/degree of the noun “hurry”; in this demonstrative use it is a demonstrative adjective.

31.explanation: Past ability is expressed by “could”: “When he was young, he could swim very well.” “can” is present tense, “would” would mark past habit, and “had to” means compulsion.

32.explanation: The sentence states a possible future result of the condition, so “might” (possibility) fits best: “The company might go bankrupt if they don’t find money quickly.” “should” is obligation, “would” needs a hypothetical condition, and “can” is ability.

34.explanation: “She could be a model” expresses present/future possibility suggested by her looks. “should” would be expectation/duty, “would” is conditional/habitual and “will” is certainty.

35.explanation: “How can I contact you?” is the usual way of asking the means of contact; “may” is a formal variant, hence medium confidence.

36.explanation: The sentence offers advice, which “should” expresses: “You should write her a letter.” “can/may/could” are possible in other senses, so medium confidence.

37.explanation: “Could I have more cheese on my sandwich?” is the polite request form. “would” and “should” do not make requests here and “must” is obligation.

38.explanation: “must” expresses obligation/necessity — passengers are required to wear their seat belts.

40.explanation: “would like to” is the polite expression of a wish: “I would like to buy the same television.”

41.explanation: An imperative with a compound predicate (“Listen” and “take notes”) still has only one independent clause, hence a simple sentence.

42.explanation: One subject and one predicate (a single clause) — simple sentence.

43.explanation: Two independent clauses — “He tried hard” and “he did not succeed” — joined by the coordinating conjunction “but” — compound sentence.

44.explanation: The subordinate clause “where the police could not trace him” depends on the main clause, so the sentence is complex.

45.explanation: A single clause expressing a comparison (“Pakistan is not so powerful as India”) — simple sentence.

46.explanation: One independent clause — simple sentence.

47.explanation: Two independent clauses — “Get in” and “you may fall ill” — joined by “or” — compound sentence.

48.explanation: The subordinate noun clause “when you went there on Sunday” qualifies “the time”, so the sentence is complex.

49.explanation: A single independent clause — simple sentence.

50.explanation: A single independent clause — simple sentence.

51.explanation: “to be understood” is an infinitive phrase completing the “too…to” construction and telling the result/manner of “speaks”, so it is adverbial. (The full “too fast to be understood” also functions adverbially.)

52.explanation: “how to solve this problem” is the object of the verb “understand”, so it is a noun phrase.

53.explanation: “like that” modifies the verb “talk” and tells the manner, so it is an adverb phrase.

54.explanation: “of means” qualifies the noun “man” (a man of means = a wealthy man), so it is an adjective phrase.

55.explanation: “of a feather” qualifies the noun “birds”, so it is an adjective phrase.

56.explanation: The infinitive phrase “How to find the way to the ruins” is the subject of the sentence, so it is a noun phrase.

57.explanation: “by means of trickery” tells how the prize was won, modifying the verb — an adverb phrase.

58.explanation: The gerund phrase “walking in the fields” is the object of “enjoy”, so it is a noun phrase.

59.explanation: “to his secret” qualifies the noun “key” (the key that opens his secret), so it is an adjective phrase.

60.explanation: “amidst many difficulties” modifies the verb “persevered”, so it is an adverb phrase.

61.explanation: The sentence contains the negative “no” (“no use”), so it is negative.

62.explanation: The sentence makes a positive statement with no negation, so it is affirmative.

63.explanation: The comparison uses the positive-degree form “so beautiful as”; the frame “No other … is so … as” is the positive-degree equivalent of the superlative, and the adjective itself is in the positive degree, so (d) Positive.

64.explanation: The sentence is marked by the negative adverb “never”, so in form it is negative. (The proverb is affirmative in sense, hence medium confidence.)

65.explanation: A plain positive statement with no negation — affirmative.

66.explanation: The verb is negated by “not” — negative.

67.explanation: “one of the most beautiful cities” uses the superlative degree of “beautiful” — superlative.

68.explanation: The adjective “stronger than any other man” is in the comparative degree; although it means the same as a superlative, its form is comparative, so (b) Comparative.

69.explanation: A positive declarative statement with no negation — affirmative, the label this paper uses for plain positive sentences (cf. Q62, Q65). “Assertive” is the wider declarative class, hence medium confidence.

70.explanation: “the highest mountain” is the superlative degree of “high” — superlative.

71.explanation: In a real future condition the if-clause takes the present simple, not the past: “He will be greatly surprised if he is felicitated by his staff members.”

72.explanation: An embedded (indirect) question drops the auxiliary inversion and uses normal order with backshifted tense: “know why the apple fell”.

73.explanation: The noun “delay” needs the adjective “inordinate”, not the adverb “inordinately”: “because of the inordinate delay”.

74.explanation: “no more room” (= no more space) is already correct and idiomatic, so no substitution improves it — (d) No improvement.

75.explanation: The subject is the singular “Each”, so the verb must be “pays”, and the traditional singular pronoun is “his”: “Each of our students pays his tuition fee…”

76.explanation: “ought” forms its negative as “ought not”, and past unfulfilled obligation is expressed by “ought not to have done”.

77.explanation: “yesterday” is past and the buying preceded the taking, so the past perfect is required: “the cycle that he had bought yesterday”.

78.explanation: The climate of Delhi must be compared with the climate of Jaipur, so the possessive “Jaipur’s” is required: “…somewhat like Jaipur’s.”

79.explanation: “beg leave of you” is correct idiomatic English meaning “ask your permission to depart”, so no improvement is needed.

80.explanation: “between” is used for exactly two people; the sentence names two thieves, so “between themselves” is correct — no improvement.

81.explanation: A boutique is a small shop that sells fashionable clothes, cosmetics and accessories.

82.explanation: “bailiwick” means one’s own area of jurisdiction or district; the sentence asks a person to stay in his own district.

83.explanation: A teetotaler abstains from all alcoholic drinks; a stoic endures without complaint, a purist insists on purity and a misogynist hates women.

84.explanation: Plagiarism is literary theft — presenting another’s words or ideas as one’s own.

85.explanation: A misologist hates learning/reason (Greek misein “to hate” + logos “reason, learning”); a misogamist hates marriage.

86.explanation: High-flown, pretentious speech is bombastic; austere means severe/simple and vituperative means abusive.

87.explanation: A pedantic style ostentatiously displays the author’s learning (pedagogy is the art of teaching, pathology the study of disease).

88.explanation: A maxim is a short pithy statement of an established principle.

89.explanation: An idiosyncrasy is a person’s peculiar habit or temperament.

90.explanation: Kleptomania is an abnormal compulsion to steal; hydrophobia is fear of water and insomnia is sleeplessness.

91.explanation: “Chronic” (long-lasting) is opposed to “acute” (short and severe) — the standard antonym pair; “temporary” is a looser opposite, hence medium confidence.

92.explanation: The proverb is “Cut your coat according to your cloth.”

93.explanation: A female pig is a sow; a doe is a female deer/rabbit, a buck a male animal and a mare a female horse.

94.explanation: “Dei gratia” is Latin for “by the grace of God”.

95.explanation: The collective noun is “a chain of mountains” (also a range).

96.explanation: The proverb is “Black will take no other hue.”

97.explanation: Taken in the sense of starting something, “launch” means “begin”; “propel/push” apply only to physically launching a projectile, so “Begin” is the intended synonym.

98.explanation: Astrology is the older pseudo-form related to Astronomy, just as Alchemy is the forerunner of Chemistry.

99.explanation: The simile is “as graceful as a swan”.

100.explanation: A filly is a young female horse; a colt is a young male, a foal a young horse of either sex and a yearling is a horse aged one year.
