1.explanation: The underlined word “Which” stands immediately before the noun “pen” and asks which one, so it functions as an interrogative adjective (determiner), not a pronoun (no noun would follow a pronoun here). Choice (b) Adjective.

2.explanation: “Became” is the past-tense form of the verb “become”; it is a linking verb joining “the dog” to the complement “mad”, so its part of speech is a verb. Choice (c) Verb.

3.explanation: “Friendship” is the object of the preposition “of” and names an abstract idea, so it is a noun. Choice (d) Noun.

4.explanation: “Very” is an adverb of degree modifying the adjective “interesting”; an adverb can modify an adjective. Choice (a) Adverb.

5.explanation: “While” links the two clauses “the mother is sleeping” and “the baby is sleeping”, so it is a subordinating conjunction. Choice (b) Conjunction.

6.explanation: “Two” is a numeral adjective modifying the noun “fingers” (it tells how many). Choice (b) Adjective.

7.explanation: “Twice” answers “how often” and modifies the verb “comes”, so it is an adverb of frequency. Choice (a) Adverb.

8.explanation: The underlined word is “next” in the phrase “next to mine”. “Next to” is a compound preposition (“We live next to the school”), so the word functions as a preposition here; it is not an adjective (nothing is being named) nor a conjunction. Choice (d) Preposition.

9.explanation: “Face” is the base form of the verb after “to learn to”, an infinitive; it names an action, so it is a verb. Choice (a) Verb.

10.explanation: “That” stands for “that book” and points back to a previously mentioned noun, so it is a demonstrative pronoun. Choice (a) Pronoun.

11.explanation: The time marker “every morning” shows a habitual present action; with the third-person singular subject “Rama”, the simple present is “goes”. Choice (d) goes.

12.explanation: “Since Monday” requires a present perfect; the subject “Jane” is singular, so “has been ill” is correct (“have been ill” would need a plural subject). Choice (a) has been ill.

13.explanation: “A week before the earthquake” places the action before another past event, so the past perfect “had left” is required. Choice (a) had left.

14.explanation: “Have you ___ today?” is the present perfect; the past participle of “write” is “written”. Choice (b) written.

15.explanation: “Gone” is the past participle used in the present perfect, which needs “has” with the singular subject “Kima”. Choice (b) has.

16.explanation: “By the time we arrive there” marks a point in the future before which the action will be complete, so the future perfect “will have reached” is correct. Choice (c) will have reached.

17.explanation: The question “By whom ___ this mess been made?” is present perfect passive; the singular subject “this mess” takes “has”. Choice (d) has.

19.explanation: “A market building” receives the action and there is no stated agent doing it now, so the passive present perfect “has been constructed” is correct. Choice (b) has been constructed.

20.explanation: “Want” is a stative verb and is not normally used in the continuous; with the singular subject “the teacher” the simple present “wants” is correct. Choice (c) wants.

21.explanation: “Beside” means “next to” and fits “waiting for me beside the road”; “besides” means “in addition to”, and “aside/asides” do not fit. Choice (b) beside.

22.explanation: The gymnast cleared the apparatus, so the preposition of movement is “over” (“jumped over the parallel bars”); “above” states position, not movement, and “atop” is not used with a motion verb here. Choice (d) over.

23.explanation: The fixed collocation is “abide by” (a rule/promise). Choice (a) by.

24.explanation: The two qualities contrast, so the coordinating conjunction “but” is needed: “rich but miserly”. Choice (b) but.

25.explanation: The sense is “not … if not”: “I shall not forgive you unless you confess”. “Unless” = if not. Choice (c) unless.

26.explanation: “Differ with” a person means to disagree with them; the topic (“with regard to this policy”) confirms the disagreement sense, so “with” is correct. Choice (d) with.

27.explanation: To “run into” someone is the idiom for meeting them by chance. Choice (a) into.

28.explanation: “Lest” introduces a negative purpose clause and takes “should”: “Work hard lest you should fail.” Choice (b) lest.

29.explanation: “Among” is used with more than two, so the money was divided among the three thieves. Choice (b) among.

30.explanation: “So that” introduces a clause of purpose: “He worked hard so that he might succeed.” Choice (d) so that.

31.explanation: “Whole” is the adjective that means the entire story: “the whole story”. “Overall”, “all” and “total” do not fit the noun phrase. Choice (a) whole.

32.explanation: The blank modifies the verb “accepted”, so an adverb is required: “happily”. “Happiness” is a noun, “happy” an adjective, and “happyly” is not a word. Choice (c) happily.

33.explanation: “In class” is a comparison among all boys, so the superlative of “tall” is needed: “the tallest boy”. Choice (d) tallest.

34.explanation: “Nearly” combines with “every one of the boys” (nearly every one); “nearly all/whole/each one” is not idiomatic here. Choice (b) every.

35.explanation: “Nearest” is the superlative adjective meaning closest to home. Choice (c) nearest.

36.explanation: The adverb “nearly” means almost and modifies “completed”: “I have nearly completed the job.” Choice (a) nearly.

37.explanation: The construction is “too … to”: “It is too hot to go out.” Choice (d) too.

38.explanation: “Aside from” is the phrase meaning “apart from/leaving out”; “Besides from”, “Except from” and “Despite from” are not correct collocations. Choice (b) Aside.

39.explanation: The comparative of the irregular adjective “bad” is “worse” (not “worst”, “worser” or “worstest”), and “much” can modify a comparative. Choice (b) worse.

41.explanation: “He will have finished the job by then” is future perfect; its interrogative moves “will” to the front and keeps the perfect participle: “Will he have finished the job by then?” Choice (d).

42.explanation: Removing “too” from “too … for words” uses the “so … that” pattern: “Her voice is so lovely that words cannot express it.” Choice (b).

43.explanation: “Few men are as wealthy as Bill Gates” means almost all others are less wealthy, so in the comparative degree “Bill Gates is wealthier than most men.” “Any other men” (b) is ungrammatical and would mean all others; (d) has a double comparative. Choice (a).

44.explanation: The comparative “better … than any other student” becomes the superlative “the best singer among the students in the school”. Choice (c).

45.explanation: Changing the affirmative “It was quite certain …” to the negative simply negates “certain”: “It was not certain that he will be found innocent.” (a) wrongly substitutes the antonym “uncertain” and (c) changes “innocent” to “guilty”. Choice (b).

46.explanation: “He does not treat any one of his daughters differently” means he treats them all the same, so the affirmative is “He treats all his daughters equally.” Choice (d).

47.explanation: The exclamatory shock at a Mizo man refusing to honour “tlawmngaihna” becomes the assertive statement “It is shameful that …”. Choice (b).

48.explanation: The adjective phrase “with great care” becomes the adverb “carefully”: “He completed the task carefully.” “Taskfully” is not a word and (b)/(c) do not replace the phrase by an adverb. Choice (d).

49.explanation: “No one will deny …” in the affirmative is “Everyone will admit …”; (c) and (d) keep the negative “not deny”. Choice (a).

50.explanation: “One of the biggest localities” is rewritten in the positive degree as “Few towns in Aizawl are as big as Dawrpui”, i.e. hardly any compare with it. Choice (b).

51.explanation: A compound sentence joins two independent clauses with a coordinating conjunction; the contrast (in spite of) needs “but”: “The boy worked hard but he didn’t succeed.” Choice (b).

53.explanation: A complex sentence needs a subordinate clause. “Because his mother was ill” is an adverb clause, giving “Alex could not go to school because his mother was ill.” (a) and (c) keep a phrase, and (b) is compound. Choice (d).

55.explanation: The compound form joins two independent clauses with “and”: “Leprosy is curable and everybody knows this.” Choice (b).

56.explanation: The simple form replaces the purpose clause “that he might pass” with an infinitive: “He worked hard to pass the test.” Choice (c).

57.explanation: Converting to a compound sentence with a coordinating conjunction: “The boy was diligent, so he was praised by the teacher.” Choice (d).

58.explanation: A complex sentence uses a subordinate clause; the relative clause “that belonged to the king” correctly post-modifies the plural “horses” (note “which was” in (d) disagrees in number). Choice (b).

59.explanation: The simple sentence replaces the conditional clause with a participial phrase: “Being a citizen, one can vote in the election.” Choice (b).

60.explanation: The noun clause “that he was guilty” turns the sentence complex: “He admitted that he was guilty.” (d) keeps only a phrase. Choice (a).

61.explanation: The two sentences are fused with an infinitive of purpose: “I need a lot of money to support my family.” Choice (b).

62.explanation: The advice “Walk fast” exists to prevent being late, so the correct conditional is negative: “If you do not walk fast, you may be late for school.” (a) and (c) reverse the logic. Choice (d).

63.explanation: The two clauses have different subjects (the lesson / the teacher), so the passive absolute participial construction is used: “The lesson being completed, the teacher left the class.” Choice (b).

64.explanation: A noun phrase in apposition renames the noun and is set off by commas: “Shakespeare, the most famous English playwright, wrote many fine plays.” Choice (d).

65.explanation: The adjective “honest” becomes the adverb “honestly” modifying “does”: “John does his work honestly.” (b) and (d) keep phrases. Choice (a).

68.explanation: A cumulative conjunction adds information; “as well as” is cumulative: “He was stupid as well as mean.” “Yet” is adversative and “hence” causal. Choice (c).

69.explanation: Adjective clauses introduced by “which” post-modify “pen”: “my pen which was red in colour, and which was stolen”. Choice (c).

70.explanation: The “so … that … cannot” pattern becomes “too … to”: “It is too hot to play outside.” Choice (c).

71.explanation: To “call it a day” means to stop working (on something) for the day. Choice (c) to stop working on something.

72.explanation: To “get bent out of shape” means to become upset or angry. Choice (a) to be upset.

73.explanation: To “break the ice” means to relieve tension and make people feel comfortable. Choice (d) to make someone feel comfortable.

74.explanation: To “hold one’s tongue” means to stay silent. Choice (a) to keep silent.

75.explanation: “At the drop of a hat” means immediately, without any hesitation. Choice (b) without any hesitation.

76.explanation: “A piece of cake” means something very easy. Choice (b) easy.

77.explanation: To “throw caution to the wind” is to abandon caution and act boldly, i.e. to take a risk (dictionaries gloss it “start taking risks”); “to be careful” is its opposite and “to be careless” describes a state rather than the act of risking. Choice (c) to take a risk.

78.explanation: “Well-off” means rich or wealthy. Choice (a) to be rich.

79.explanation: To “pass over” something is to ignore or overlook it. Choice (d) to overlook.

80.explanation: To “take to one’s heels” means to run away. Choice (d) to run away.

81.explanation: “Sorrow” (deep sadness) is closest in meaning to “grief”; “joy” is its opposite. Choice (b) grief.

82.explanation: “Insolent” means boldly rude or disrespectful, i.e. ill-mannered; “polite” is its opposite. Choice (a) ill-mannered.

83.explanation: “Perpetual” means continuing forever, i.e. permanent; “temporary” is its opposite. Choice (d) permanent.

84.explanation: “Yearn” means to long for or desire strongly. Choice (a) desire.

85.explanation: “Contrary” means opposite or opposed. Choice (a) opposite.

86.explanation: “Precede” means to come before; its antonym is “succeed” (to come after). “Before” is a synonym. Choice (a) succeed.

87.explanation: “Magnify” means to enlarge or increase; its antonym is “reduce”. Choice (c) reduce.

88.explanation: “Confess” means to admit; its antonym is “deny”. “Profess” is close to confess, not opposite. Choice (d) deny.

89.explanation: “Lenient” means merciful or not strict; its antonym is “strict”. “Relaxed” is a synonym. Choice (a) strict.

90.explanation: “Advance” means to move forward; its antonym is “retreat”. “Forward” is a synonym. Choice (b) retreat.

92.explanation: “Edible” means fit to be eaten. Choice (a) Fit to be eaten.

93.explanation: A “teetotaller” is a person who does not drink alcohol. Choice (b) One who does not drink alcohol.

94.explanation: “Insatiable” means that cannot be satisfied (of a desire or need). Choice (b) Cannot be satisfied.

95.explanation: “Obnoxious” means unpleasant or offensive. Choice (a) Unpleasant.

96.explanation: “Indefatigable” means tireless or untiring. Choice (b) Untiring.

97.explanation: “Posthumously” means after death (of a work published after the author’s death). Choice (d) After his death.

98.explanation: A “virtuoso” is a person highly skilled in an art, i.e. an expert. Choice (a) Expert.

99.explanation: “Impregnable” means unable to be captured or broken into; of the choices, (d) “Cannot be destroyed” is the only one giving the positive sense (the others say not fortified, unguarded, decayed). Choice (d) Cannot be destroyed.

100.explanation: “Nepotism” is the practice of favouring one’s relatives or friends, especially in giving jobs. Choice (b) Favouring one’s relatives.

1.explanation: In “a few boys” the word “few” tells how many boys there are and modifies the noun “boys”; a word that qualifies a noun is an adjective (an adjective of number/quantity), so (c) Adjective.

2.explanation: “Laughter” names the thing that “fills the air” and is the object of the preposition “of”; a naming word is a noun, so (a) Noun.

3.explanation: “Someone” stands in place of an unspecified person and is the subject of “has broken”; a word used in place of a noun is a pronoun (indefinite pronoun), so (b) Pronoun.

4.explanation: “Always” answers the question “how often?” about the verb “help” and can be removed without breaking the sentence; a word that modifies a verb is an adverb, so (c) Adverb.

5.explanation: “Within” relates the verb “return” to the noun phrase “a week” (within what period), so it is a preposition, (b).

6.explanation: “Among” relates the passive verb “was divided” to “the thieves” (distribution to more than two), so it is a preposition, (d). “Between” is used for two.

7.explanation: “Crowd” is the subject of “had gathered” and names a group of people; it is a noun, (a).

8.explanation: “Though” joins the subordinate clause “he worked hard” to the main clause “he failed” and expresses concession; a joining word is a conjunction, (b).

9.explanation: “Huge” qualifies the noun “caterpillar” (what kind of caterpillar), so it is an adjective, (a).

10.explanation: “Must” is a modal auxiliary that combines with the main verb “finish” (“must finish”) to express necessity; it belongs to the verb class, so (c) Verb.

11.explanation: “Among” is used when something is distributed to more than two people (“the children”); “between” is for two, so (c) among.

12.explanation: A day or date takes “on”: “born on Thursday, 12th March”, so (d) on.

13.explanation: One lives “above” someone when the flat is on a higher floor; “above mine” is the usual idiom for the flat directly overhead, so (a) above. “Over” is not used for floors.

14.explanation: “Beside” means “at the side of”: “sitting beside the road” (d). “Besides” means “in addition to”, “aside”/“astride” do not fit.

15.explanation: “For” is used with a length of time: “working for five hours”; “since” needs a point of time, so (a) for.

16.explanation: The instrument of a passive action takes “with”: “beaten with a stick”, so (b) with. “By” would name the agent.

17.explanation: “Within a week” means before the week is over, so (c) within.

18.explanation: “Abide” takes the fixed preposition “by”: “abide by the rules”, so (d) by.

19.explanation: “A disgrace to his family” is the fixed expression, so (b) to.

20.explanation: “Blind to” is the fixed expression meaning unable to see/notice: “blind to the faults”, so (a) to.

21.explanation: The blank follows “the” and depends on “of his watch”, so a noun is required: “the loss of his watch”. “Lost/lose/loose” are verb/participle/adjective forms, so (d) loss.

22.explanation: “Since this morning” marks an action that started in the past and is still going on, which needs the present perfect continuous: “I have been waiting”, so (a).

23.explanation: “Daily” signals a habitual present action, and the subject “He” takes the singular present “takes”, so (a).

24.explanation: “While” introduces an action going on at the same moment, so the present continuous “is doing” fits: “while he is doing his homework”, so (c).

26.explanation: “When we reached the church” fixes a past moment, and the service had already begun before it, so the past perfect “had already started” is required, (c).

27.explanation: The sentence reports a single completed theft, not a habit, so the past perfect “had stolen” is the appropriate form, (c). Simple present “steals” would describe a repeated habit.

28.explanation: After the auxiliary “has” a past participle is required, and the participle of “hurt” is “hurt”: “has hurt me deeply”, so (b).

29.explanation: “Right now” marks an action happening at the moment of speaking, so the present continuous “is raining” is required, (a).

30.explanation: “Have you ever …” takes a past participle; the participle of “sing” is “sung”, so (c).

31.explanation: The two clauses contrast (“tried his best” / “could not succeed”); the coordinating conjunction “but” joins them, so (c). “Yet”/“still” are possible in other positions but the printed single blank needs “but”.

32.explanation: The second clause gives the reason for allowing the person to go (“your teacher has not come”), so the causal conjunction “since” fits, (d). “Lest” would need a subjunctive, and “and/but” do not express the reason.

33.explanation: The sentence concedes that he ran fast and still missed the bus; the concessive conjunction is “though”, so (d). “Since/as/because” would reverse the logic.

34.explanation: “As soon as you reach home” means at the moment you arrive, so (c) as soon as.

35.explanation: “Unless you confess” means if you do not confess; it gives the condition for not pardoning, so (c) unless.

36.explanation: “Nearly” means almost; “I nearly hit him” (I almost hit him) is the sense required, so (a). “Completely hit him” would mean he was fully struck, which contradicts “this morning” being an accident.

37.explanation: “Words” is a plural countable noun, so “few” is used: “a few words”, (a). “Little” goes with uncountables.

38.explanation: The sentence asks which one of the pens belongs to the listener: “which pen is yours”, so (d) which. “Whose pen is yours?” is not logical, and “what/those” are ungrammatical here.

39.explanation: “Books” is countable plural, so “how many books” is correct, (b). “Much” goes with uncountables.

40.explanation: “Hard” is both adjective and adverb meaning “with effort”: “He works hard”, so (c). “Hardly” means scarcely, and the other two are not words.

41.explanation: “Finishing my paper” is a participial phrase (not a clause) attached to the single subject “I”, and “I gave it to the teacher” is one independent clause, so the sentence is simple, (c).

42.explanation: “Everyone knows” is the main clause and “that the earth is round” is a noun clause acting as its object; a main clause plus a subordinate clause makes a complex sentence, so (a).

43.explanation: “I have sold my cow” is the main clause and “which was black in colour” is a subordinate relative (adjectival) clause; a main clause with a dependent clause is a complex sentence, so (c). Option (b) names the clause, not the sentence.

44.explanation: “That he cannot stand” is a noun clause: “that” introduces a clause that functions as a noun (as the subject or object of an unstated main clause). It is not itself a simple or complex sentence, so (c) Noun clause.

46.explanation: “To compound” needs a coordinating link joining the two facts. “He was not only punished but fined also” coordinates the two facts with the correlative “not only … but … also”, so (b). Options (a) and (c) are participial phrases (simple), and (d) merely joins two bare predicates with “and” and does not use the correlative pattern the transform calls for.

47.explanation: “To simple” requires one clause. “He is dishonest and not liked by anybody” is a single subject (“He”) with two coordinated predicates, i.e. a simple sentence, so (c). Option (a) “Being dishonest, nobody likes him” is a dangling participle (the participial phrase would have to modify “nobody”, which it cannot), so it is not the correct simple sentence.

50.explanation: “To complex” needs a main clause plus a subordinate clause. “He worked so hard that his health broke down” contains the result adverb clause “that his health broke down”, so (b). (a) is compound, and (c)/(d) are simple.

51.explanation: With “since” = because, the clause that gives the reason must be “I am at fault”: “I must be punished since I am at fault”, so (b). Options (a) and (d) reverse the cause and (c) is malformed.

53.explanation: “To take” is the infinitive, and the “too … to” pattern expresses the result: “It is too cold to take a bath”, so (c). (a), (b) and (d) contain no infinitive construction of the required type.

54.explanation: “Either … or” joins the two names as the subject: “Either John or Jacob has done it”, so (d). (a) and (c) misplace the correlatives and (b) has no finite verb.

55.explanation: “For” here means “because” and must introduce the reason clause: “I cannot read his note-book for his hand writing is poor”, so (a).

57.explanation: The participial construction is the absolute “The movie being over, …”: “The movie being over, the audience went out of the theatre”, so (b). (a), (c) and (d) use full clauses.

58.explanation: The facts are that he worked hard and still failed, so the concessive clause must be “he worked hard”: “He failed though he worked hard”, so (d). Options (a) and (b) reverse the concession.

59.explanation: The infinitive “to hear” is needed after “overjoyed”: “My father is overjoyed to hear of my success”, so (c). (a) uses “too … to” and changes the sense.

60.explanation: “Not only … but also” must join the two complements after the verb: “She is not only beautiful, but also charming”, so (b). (a) has wrong word order and (d) is malformed.

61.explanation: “You are a lazy boy.” states a fact in the affirmative, so its notion is affirmative/declarative, (a) Affirmative.

63.explanation: “She visits her grandmother during the holidays.” makes a statement, so it is assertive, (c).

64.explanation: “Fetch me my slippers at once” gives a command, so it is imperative, (d).

65.explanation: “Please take me with you” makes a request/command, so it is imperative, (a).

66.explanation: The exclamation “What a dreadful smell!” asserts that something is a dreadful smell: “It is a dreadful smell”, so (b). (a) is a fragment and (d) loses the description.

67.explanation: To make it interrogative, the auxiliary “does” is used with the subject: “Does every rose have its thorn?”, so (a). (b) keeps the wrong verb form, (c)/(d) are ungrammatical.

68.explanation: The question “Have you done your homework?” becomes the statement “You have done your homework”, so (c). (a)/(b) change the mood and (d) remains a question.

69.explanation: The imperative “Hurry up.” becomes the polite request-question “Can you please hurry up?”, so (c). (a) shifts to the past and (b)/(d) are not questions.

70.explanation: The polite question “Will you please close the door?” becomes the imperative “Close the door, please.”, so (a). (b) is a statement and (c)/(d) are optative.

71.explanation: “Drawn near to death” means approaching death, i.e. “to approach”, (b).

72.explanation: “Come to light” means to become known/revealed, so (d) to become known.

73.explanation: “To beat about the bush” means to talk around the point without coming to it, so (a).

74.explanation: “To do without luxury items” means to manage or live without them, so (c) to live without something.

75.explanation: “In hot water” means in trouble/difficulty, so (c) to be in trouble.

76.explanation: “To give herself airs” means to behave as if she is superior, i.e. to boast, so (c).

77.explanation: “To hold his own” means to keep up one’s position / not be defeated, so (b) to keep up one’s position.

78.explanation: “Better-half” is a jocular term for one’s wife/husband; in “his better-half” it means his wife, so (b).

79.explanation: A “close-fisted man” is one who is unwilling to spend, i.e. a miser, so (b).

80.explanation: “At daggers drawn” means in bitter enmity, so (d) bitter enemies.

81.explanation: “Conscious of” means aware of, so the synonym is (a) aware. “Oblivious” is the opposite.

82.explanation: “Reclusive” means avoiding the company of others, so the nearest meaning is (d) avoiding society.

83.explanation: “Invincible” means too strong to be defeated, so the synonym is (c) undefeatable. “Invisible” sounds similar but means unseen.

84.explanation: “Inevitable” means that which cannot be avoided, so the synonym is (b) unavoidable.

85.explanation: “Apathy” means lack of interest/feeling, so the synonym is (b) indifference. “Sympathy/empathy” are near-opposites.

86.explanation: “Candid” means frank/open; its opposite is (b) dishonest (not open). “Frank” is a synonym.

87.explanation: “Pompous” means self-important/arrogant; its opposite is (d) humble. “Proud/boastful” are synonyms.

88.explanation: “Credible” means believable; its opposite is (a) unbelievable. “Believable” is a synonym.

89.explanation: “Inaccessible” means not reachable/approachable; its opposite is (a) approachable. “Unapproachable” is a synonym.

90.explanation: “Genuine” means real/sincere; its opposite is (d) fake. “Real/truthful” are synonyms.

91.explanation: Espionage is the practice of spying or using spies, so (b).

92.explanation: A linguist is a scholar of language(s), so (c) scholar of many languages.

93.explanation: A philanderer is a man who pursues many women (a). “Investigator” and “copier” describe other words.

94.explanation: Utopia is an imagined place where everything is perfect, so (a).

95.explanation: Simultaneous means happening at the same time, so (c).

96.explanation: Oblivious means unaware of what is happening around one, so (c).

97.explanation: Incorrigible means that which cannot be corrected, so (d).

98.explanation: A precedent is an earlier event regarded as a guide to subsequent similar events, so (c).

99.explanation: A bigot is a person intolerant of others holding different beliefs, so (c).

100.explanation: Conclusion is the end of an event or process, so (b).

1.direction: Directions (Questions 1-12) : Read the following passage carefully and choose the correct answer to

opts.a: Duties without rights are mere slavery
opts.b: Rights without duties amount to lawlessness
opts.c: Both are part of a civilized society

1.q: Why are rights and duties called two sides of the same coin?
1.passage: Rights and duties are two sides of the same coin. One can’t exist without the other. Duties without rights are merely slavery. Similarly, rights without duties amount to lawlessness. In any civilized society, rights and duties must go side by side. But in today’s world, everybody talks much about his rights. There is a great hue and cry if our rights are infringed. But nobody seems to bother much about his duties. That is why there is great unrest in our present-day life. Actually duties come first, and rights afterwards. Many a time one man’s rights is another man’s duty and vice versa. For example, every man has the right to have an undisturbed sleep. So it becomes the duty of his neighbour not to tune his radio at too high a pitch. If we want to enjoy our rights we should act in such a way that the rights of others are not trespassed. It can happen only if we take due account of our duties also. In short, rights and duties are complementary things and not contradictory. It is difficult to agree on which rights should be guaranteed to a citizen. For example, does a child have the right to be educated in his/her mother tongue? Some enthusiasts may say, “Certainly”. But others may say that while everyone must have a right to education, the government should not be enforced to spend money to employ teachers for the language of every group and community. Take another example. Does every adult have a right to a job? Some will say, “Yes”. Other will disagree and say that this is a privilege, not a right. They say that in these days of population explosion, it is not possible for any government to ensure full employment. There can be disagreement on such controversial issues, but there can be no disagreement on such things as the freedom of speech, freedom of religion, freedom from want and freedom from fear. Every nation worth the name must ensure these rights for her citizens.
1.explanation: The passage explicitly says duties without rights are slavery and rights without duties are lawlessness.

17.q: The antonym of indolent is:
17.passage: I designed, after my first voyage, to spend the rest of my days at Baghdad, but it was not long ere I grew weary of an indolent life, and I put to sea a second time, with merchants of known probity. We embarked on board of a good ship, and after recommending ourselves to God, set sail. One day we landed on an island covered with several sorts of fruit-trees, but we could see neither man nor animal. We walked in the meadows, along the streams that watered them. Whilst some diverted themselves with gathering flowers, and other fruits, I took my wine and provisions, and set down near a stream betwixt two high trees, which afforded a delightful shade. I made a good meal, and afterwards fell asleep. I cannot tell how long I slept, but when I awoke the ship was no longer in view. In this sad condition, I was ready to die with grief. I cried out in agony, beat my head and breast, and threw myself upon the ground, where I lay some time, overwhelmed by a rushing current of thoughts, each more distressing than the last. When I gazed towards the sea I could discern nothing but sky and water; but looking over the land I beheld something white; and coming down, I took what provision I had left, and went towards the object, which was so distant that at first could not distinguish what it was. As I approached, I thought it to be a white dome, of a prodigious height and extent. I drew near to it, and walked round it; but found no door to it; and I found that I had not strength nor activity to climb it, on account of its exceeding smoothness. I made a mark at the place where I stood, and went around the dome, measuring its circumference; and lo! It was fifty full paces; and I meditated upon some means of gaining an entrance into it; but no means of accomplishing this occurred to me. By this time the sun was about to set, and all of a sudden the sky became as dark as if it had been covered with a thick cloud. I was much astonished at this sudden darkness but much more when I found it occasioned by a bird of most extraordinary size, that came flying towards me. I remembered that I had often heard mariners speak of a miraculous bird called the roc, and conceived that the great dome which I so much admired must be her egg. Shortly afterwards, the bird alighted, and sat over the egg.

27.q: The antonym of MISERABLE is:
27.passage: Many men and women are so money minded that they do not undertake any serious work that does not pay. They believe that it is foolish to exert themselves for study and brain work which cannot be converted into cash. ‘Hard work only for money, and then plenty of play and pleasure’: this seems to be their rule of life. They value intellect only as the key to material prosperity and regard personal mental development as a foolish fad. This miserable materialistic psychology is very deep rooted in all classes of society. Rich and poor, all suffer from it. An old working woman complained to me of her son’s habit of occasionally buying some books, and said, “He wastes his money on books. What good are they to him? He is a carpenter, not a schoolmaster”.

1.q: The main focus of the passage is on the plight of
1.passage: Though the U.S prides itself on being a leader in the world community, a recent report shows that it lags far behind other industrialised countries in meeting the needs of its youngest and most vulnerable citizens. The U.S has a higher infant-mortality rate, a higher proportion of low birth weight babies, a smaller proportion of babies immunized against childhood diseases and a much higher rate of adolescent pregnancies. These findings, described as a ‘quiet crisis’requiring immediate and far-reaching action, appeared in a report prepared by a task force of educators, doctors, politicians and business people. According to the report, a fourth of the nation’s 12 million infants and toddlers live in poverty. As many as half confront risk factors that could harm their ability to develop intellectually, physically and socially. Child immunizations are too low, more children are born into poverty, more are in substandard care while their parents work and more are being raised by single parents. When taken together, these and other risk factors can lead to educational and health problems that are much harder and are more costly to reverse. The crisis began in the womb with unplanned parenthood. Women with unplanned pregnancies are less likely to seek pre-natal care. In the U.S 80% of teenage pregnancies and 56% of all pregnancies are unplanned. The problems continue after birth where unplanned pregnancies and unstable partnerships often go hand in hand. Since 1950, the number of single parent families has nearly tripled. More than 25 percent of all births today are to unmarried mothers. As the number of single parent families grow and more women enter the work force, infants and toddlers are increasingly in the care of people other than their parents. Most disturbingly, recent statistics show that American parents are increasingly neglecting or abusing their children. In only four years from 1987-1991, the number of children in foster care increased by over 50 percent. Babies under the age of one are the fastest growing category of children entering foster care. The crisis affects children under the age of three most severely, the report says. Yet, it is this period-from infancy through pre-school years-that sets the stage for child’s future.

These findings, described as a ‘quiet crisis’requiring immediate and far-reaching action, appeared in a report prepared by a task force of educators, doctors, politicians and business people. According to the report, a fourth of the nation’s 12 million infants and toddlers live in poverty. As many as half confront risk factors that could harm their ability to develop intellectually, physically and socially. Child immunizations are too low, more children are born into poverty, more are in substandard care while their parents work and more are being raised by single parents. When taken together, these and other risk factors can lead to educational and health problems that are much harder and are more costly to reverse. The crisis began in the womb with unplanned parenthood. Women with unplanned pregnancies are less likely to seek pre-natal care. In the U.S 80% of teenage pregnancies and 56% of all pregnancies are unplanned. The problems continue after birth where unplanned pregnancies and unstable partnerships often go hand in hand. Since 1950, the number of single parent families has nearly tripled. More than 25 percent of all births today are to unmarried mothers. As the number of single parent families grow and more women enter the work force, infants and toddlers are increasingly in the care of people other than their parents. Most disturbingly, recent statistics show that American parents are increasingly neglecting or abusing their children. In only four years from 1987-1991, the number of children in foster care increased by over 50 percent. Babies under the age of one are the fastest growing category of children entering foster care. The crisis affects children under the age of three most severely, the report says. Yet, it is this period-from infancy through pre-school years-that sets the stage for child’s future.
3.explanation: The passage gives no information about foster-care numbers after 1991. Option (b), “has decreased after 1991,” is unsupported rather than contradicted; the question asks which statement is not true, so the text does not establish a unique answer.
3.reviewNote: Held because the passage does not provide enough evidence to determine a unique statement.

1.explanation: The passage focuses on conditions affecting infants and toddlers.

2.explanation: Normal birth weight is not a crisis factor; the passage reports a higher proportion of low-birth-weight babies.

4.explanation: Vulnerable means susceptible to harm.

5.explanation: The passage identifies lack of adequate care and poverty among risk factors; it does not identify parental illiteracy.

6.explanation: It says women with unplanned pregnancies are less likely to seek prenatal care.

7.explanation: The passage combines long-term trends from 1950 with statistics through the contemporary period.

8.explanation: Babies under one year are identified as the fastest-growing foster-care category.

9.explanation: To cry wolf is to raise a false alarm.

10.explanation: Above board means honest or legitimate.

11.explanation: To drive a point home is to emphasize it.

12.explanation: Having an axe to grind means having a private interest or purpose.

13.explanation: To kick the bucket means to die.

14.explanation: To cut someone short means to interrupt them.

15.explanation: A bolt from the blue is a complete surprise.

16.explanation: Plain sailing means smooth, easy progress.

17.explanation: To take to one’s heels means to run away.

18.explanation: To toe the line is to comply with rules or expectations.

19.explanation: To tread on someone’s toes is to offend them.

20.explanation: Much ado about nothing means making a fuss over a small matter.

21.explanation: An apple of discord is a cause of contention.

22.explanation: Washing dirty linen in public means exposing private quarrels publicly.

23.explanation: To rub shoulders with someone is to meet or come into contact with them.

24.explanation: To get cold feet is to become afraid or lose nerve.

25.explanation: To lag behind is to move slowly; rushing is the opposite.

26.explanation: To confront is to face; evade is the opposite.

27.explanation: To develop is to grow; repress is the opposite.

28.explanation: To reverse is to turn back; to advance is the opposite.

29.explanation: Stagnant describes something not changing, the opposite of unstable.

30.explanation: Abusing/ill-treating is opposed to praising or acclaiming.

31.explanation: A crisis is a time of difficulty; calm is the opposite state.

32.explanation: Severely means to a great degree; slightly is the opposite.

33.explanation: “Usually” modifies the verb “eat,” so it is an adverb.

34.explanation: “Innocence” names a quality, so it is a noun.

35.explanation: “Upon” introduces the object “the injured deer,” so it is a preposition.

36.explanation: “Match” names the thing won, so it is a noun.

37.explanation: “And” joins clauses, so it is a conjunction.

38.explanation: “Enough” modifies the adjective/adverb “loud,” so it is an adverb.

39.explanation: “Invincible” describes “courage,” so it is an adjective.

40.explanation: “Alas!” expresses emotion and is an interjection.

41.explanation: The collocation is “fatal to his reputation and health.”

42.explanation: The phrase is “embark upon a programme.”

43.explanation: One is vexed at a reply or situation.

44.explanation: A visit advanced by two days is moved earlier by two days.

45.explanation: Inured takes the preposition “to.”

46.explanation: The collocation is “pin one’s hopes on” something.

47.explanation: To be cut out for a job is to be suited to it.

48.explanation: “Have no scruples in doing something” is acceptable usage; “about” would be more usual but is not offered.

49.explanation: It has two independent clauses joined by “or,” so it is compound (though the first also contains a subordinate clause).

50.explanation: Two independent clauses are joined by “and,” making it compound.

51.explanation: The infinitive phrase “to make up…” is not an independent clause; the sentence is simple.

52.explanation: “So that he might win” is a subordinate purpose clause, making it complex.

53.explanation: One independent clause; simple sentence.

54.explanation: The “If…” subordinate clause depends on the main clause, making it complex.

55.explanation: Two independent clauses are joined by “but,” making it compound.

56.explanation: “Which belonged to his uncle” is a subordinate relative clause, making it complex.

57.explanation: “As soon as the mails arrive” is a subordinate time clause, making it complex.

58.explanation: One independent clause; simple sentence.

59.explanation: “No” makes the assertion negative.

60.explanation: It states a positive fact and is affirmative.

61.explanation: The exclamation mark and wording make it exclamatory.

62.explanation: It gives a command, so it is imperative.

63.explanation: It asks a question and is interrogative.

64.explanation: It makes a declarative assertion, so it is assertive.

65.explanation: “Auspicious occasion” means a favorable or propitious occasion.

66.explanation: The trader was detained by authorities.

67.explanation: A spoiled child may become sullen when attention is withheld.

68.explanation: Explicit directions are clear and detailed.

69.explanation: To reappear for an examination is to sit it again.

70.explanation: A victorious team is welcomed by a jubilant (joyful) crowd.

71.explanation: The natural collocation is “render help.”

72.explanation: To put down a rebellion is to suppress it.

73.explanation: Furtive means secret or concealed.

74.explanation: Pensive means absorbed in thought; thoughtful is closest.

75.explanation: A penchant is a strong inclination or liking.

76.explanation: Paucity means scarcity.

77.explanation: Famished means extremely hungry.

78.explanation: A reprimand is a rebuke.

79.explanation: Respite means a period of relief.

80.explanation: Disparate results are different from one another.

archive-lang-2020-informatics-officer-un.evidence: Compared all 100 Section B questions with the scanned eight-page General English Paper-II. The cover identifies Informatics Officer under Information & Communication Technology Department, February 2021, 2 hours, 100 marks and one mark per question. Visually checked the underlined targets and option order on pages 1, 5 and 6; checked numbering and remaining printed text on all pages. No MPSC answer key is published for this sitting. Q1’s OCR emphasis was corrected from “any” to the printed underlined “that”. Source-preserved duplicate Q71 options.

1.direction: Direction (Questions No. 1 - 10) : Identify the parts of speech of the underlined words :
1.q: Take any magazine **that** you like.
1.explanation: “That” introduces the relative clause “that you like” and stands for “magazine”; it is a relative pronoun.

2.direction: Direction (Questions No. 1 - 10) : Identify the parts of speech of the underlined words :
2.q: She went away **before** he came.
2.explanation: “Before” joins the clauses “She went away” and “he came”, so it is a subordinating conjunction.

3.direction: Direction (Questions No. 1 - 10) : Identify the parts of speech of the underlined words :
3.q: He cannot **even** see me.
3.explanation: “Even” modifies “see” by emphasizing the verb; it is an adverb.

4.direction: Direction (Questions No. 1 - 10) : Identify the parts of speech of the underlined words :
4.q: He was much loved **by** his wife.
4.explanation: “By” introduces the agent “his wife” in a passive construction; it is a preposition.

5.direction: Direction (Questions No. 1 - 10) : Identify the parts of speech of the underlined words :
5.q: He conceived a **master** plan.
5.explanation: “Master” modifies the noun “plan”; it is an adjective.

6.direction: Direction (Questions No. 1 - 10) : Identify the parts of speech of the underlined words :
6.q: **One** would think he was mad.
6.explanation: “One” stands for a person in general and is used pronominally as the subject.

7.direction: Direction (Questions No. 1 - 10) : Identify the parts of speech of the underlined words :
7.q: Do not **back** false friends.
7.explanation: “Back” means support and is the main verb in “Do not back false friends.”

8.direction: Direction (Questions No. 1 - 10) : Identify the parts of speech of the underlined words :
8.q: She fell down into the **deep**.
8.explanation: “The deep” means the deep sea or a deep place; “deep” is a noun here.

9.direction: Direction (Questions No. 1 - 10) : Identify the parts of speech of the underlined words :
9.q: He likes this more **than** that.
9.explanation: “Than” links the compared alternatives in “more than”; it is a conjunction in this construction.

10.direction: Direction (Questions No. 1 - 10) : Identify the parts of speech of the underlined words :
10.q: The man was in a terrible **fix**.
10.explanation: “Fix” names a difficult predicament; it is a noun.

11.direction: Direction (Questions No. 11 - 20) : Fill in the blanks with appropriate prepositions.
11.q: There was a very serious accident __________ the roundabout.
11.explanation: The idiomatic location is “at the roundabout.”

12.direction: Direction (Questions No. 11 - 20) : Fill in the blanks with appropriate prepositions.
12.q: In many countries people drive __________ the left.
12.explanation: The standard expression is “drive on the left.”

13.direction: Direction (Questions No. 11 - 20) : Fill in the blanks with appropriate prepositions.
13.q: To reach their village, they have to change __________ a small train at the junction.
13.explanation: When changing trains, one changes “to” the connecting train.

14.direction: Direction (Questions No. 11 - 20) : Fill in the blanks with appropriate prepositions.
14.q: There was nothing he could do __________ wait.
14.explanation: “There was nothing he could do except wait” means waiting was the only option.

15.direction: Direction (Questions No. 11 - 20) : Fill in the blanks with appropriate prepositions.
15.q: If you live in a corrupt society, you cannot easily rise __________ the prevailing corruption.
15.explanation: “Rise above” means overcome or avoid being controlled by something.

16.direction: Direction (Questions No. 11 - 20) : Fill in the blanks with appropriate prepositions.
16.q: A jeep hit him while he was going __________ main road.
16.explanation: The intended phrase is “on the main road”; the scan omits “the”, but “on” is the only suitable preposition.

17.direction: Direction (Questions No. 11 - 20) : Fill in the blanks with appropriate prepositions.
17.q: The bridge __________ this river was built in the year 1995.
17.explanation: A bridge is built “over” a river.

18.direction: Direction (Questions No. 11 - 20) : Fill in the blanks with appropriate prepositions.
18.q: We hadn’t had anything to eat __________ the journey.
18.explanation: “During the journey” locates the period when they had nothing to eat.

19.direction: Direction (Questions No. 11 - 20) : Fill in the blanks with appropriate prepositions.
19.q: He is quick __________ solving questions.
19.explanation: The usual collocation is “quick at” doing something.

20.direction: Direction (Questions No. 11 - 20) : Fill in the blanks with appropriate prepositions.
20.q: We must not fight __________ our friends.
20.explanation: “Fight with our friends” means quarrel with them.

21.direction: Direction (Questions No. 21 - 30) : Indicate the mood of the given sentences.
21.q: I may go to the beach later.
21.explanation: This is a statement about a possible future action, so it is indicative.

22.direction: Direction (Questions No. 21 - 30) : Indicate the mood of the given sentences.
22.q: Science is fascinating.
22.explanation: “Science is fascinating” is a declarative statement in the indicative mood.

23.direction: Direction (Questions No. 21 - 30) : Indicate the mood of the given sentences.
23.q: Stop writing, put your pens down.
23.explanation: “Stop writing, put your pens down” gives commands, so it is imperative.

24.direction: Direction (Questions No. 21 - 30) : Indicate the mood of the given sentences.
24.q: Have you found your book?
24.explanation: The question asks whether an event occurred; it uses the indicative mood.

25.direction: Direction (Questions No. 21 - 30) : Indicate the mood of the given sentences.
25.q: They came to speak to me.
25.explanation: The main verb “came” makes this a declarative statement in the indicative; “to speak” is an infinitive phrase, not the sentence mood.

26.direction: Direction (Questions No. 21 - 30) : Indicate the mood of the given sentences.
26.q: God bless you!
26.explanation: “God bless you!” expresses a wish; the bare verb “bless” is subjunctive in this optative use.

27.direction: Direction (Questions No. 21 - 30) : Indicate the mood of the given sentences.
27.q: Do sit down.
27.explanation: “Do sit down” is a polite command, hence imperative.

The first thing the children wanted to do at the zoo was to ride the elephant. They were frightened as they climbed the ladder to take their seats on the swaying back of the huge beast. Elephants seem awkward creatures as they move along heavily, their legs covered with loose folds of tough skin and their trunk swinging from side to side in search of food or drink. After their ride on the elephant, the children went to see the lions and tigers. Crowds of people stood watching, protected from the cruel beasts by the strong metal bars of the cages.

In the end, they saw some curious creatures like the giraffe with its long neck and the camel with its short beard.

8.passage: Most of us use the products of science — railways, aeroplanes, electricity, wireless and thousands of others — without thinking how they came into existence. We take them for granted, as if we were entitled to them as a matter of right. We are very proud of the fact that we live in an advanced age and are ourselves very advanced. Now, there is no doubt that our age is very different from previous ages and I think it is perfectly correct to say that it is far more advanced. But it is a different thing from saying that we, as individuals or groups, are more advanced. It would be the height of absurdity to say that because an engine driver can run an engine and Plato or Socrates could not, the engine driver is more advanced than, or is superior to, Plato or Socrates. But it would be perfectly correct to say that the engine itself is a more advanced method of locomotion than Plato’s chariot was.

17.passage:
People talk of memorials to him in statues of bronze or marble or pillars and thus they mock him and belie his message. What tribute shall we pay to him that he would have appreciated? He has shown us the way to live and the way to die and if we have not understood that lesson it would be better that we raised no memorial to him, for only fit memorial is to follow reverently in the path he showed us and to do our duty in life and in death.

He was a Hindu and an Indian, the greatest in many generations, and he was proud of being a Hindu and an Indian. To him India was dear because she had represented throughout the ages certain immutable truths. But though he was intensely religious and came to be called the father of the Nation which he had liberated, yet no narrow religious or national bonds confined his spirit. And so he became the great internationalist, believing in the essential unity of man, the underlying unity of all religions, and the needs of humanity, and more specially devoting himself to the service of the poor, the distressed and the oppressed millions everywhere.

His death brought more tributes than have been paid at the passing of any other human being in history. Perhaps what would have pleased him best was the spontaneous tributes that came from the people of Pakistan. 1.passage:
Philosophy of Education is a labelapplied to the study of the purpose, process, nature and
     ideals of education. It can be considered a branch of both philosophy and education. Education
     can be defined as the teaching and learning of specific skills, and the imparting of knowledge,
     judgment and wisdom, and is something broader than the societal institution of education we
     often speak of. Many educationalists consider it a weak and woolly field, too far removed from
     the practical applications of the real world to be useful. But philosophers dating back to Plato
     and the Ancient Greeks have given the area much thought and emphasis, and there is little doubt
     that their work has helped shape the practice of education over the millennia.
           Plato is the earliest important educational thinker, and education is an essential element in
     “The Republic” (his most important work on philosophy and political theory, written around
     360 B.C.). In it, he advocates some rather extreme methods: removing children from their mothers’
     care and raising them as wards of the state, and differentiating children suitable to the various
     castes, the highest receiving the most education, so that they could act as guardians of the city
     and care for the less able. He believed that education should be holistic, including facts, skills,
     physical discipline, music and art. Plato’s beliefs regarding education was very democratic in
     that he believed that talent and intelligence is not distributed genetically and thus is be found in
     children born to all classes; however, his proposed system of selective public education for an
     educated minority of the population does not really follow a democratic model.
                                               -2-

         Aristotle considered human nature, habit and reason to be equally important forces to be
   cultivated in education, the ultimate aim of which should be to produce good and virtuous
   citizens. He proposed that teachers lead their students systematically, and that repetition be
   used as a key tool to develop good habits, unlike Socrates’ emphasis on questioning his listeners
   to bring out their own ideas. He emphasized the balancing of the theoretical and practical
   aspects of subjects taught, among which he explicitly mentions reading, writing, mathematics,
   music, physical education, literature, history, and a wide range of sciences, as well as play,
   which he also considered important.
        During the Medieval period, the idea of Perennialism was first formulated by St. Thomas
   Aquinas in his work “De Magistro”. Perennialism holds that one should teach those things
   deemed to be of everlasting importance to all people everywhere, namely principles and
   reasoning, not just facts (which are apt to change over time), and that one should teach first
   about people, not machines or techniques. It was originally religious in nature, and it was only
   much later that a theory of secular perennialism developed.
         During the Renaissance, the French skeptic Michel de Montaigne (1533 - 1592) was one
   of the first to critically look at education. Unusually for his time, Montaigne was willing to
   question the conventional wisdom of the period, calling into question the whole edifice of the
   educational system, and the implicit assumption that university-educated philosophers were
   necessarily wiser than uneducated farm workers, for example.

     can be defined as the teaching and learning of specific skills, and the imparting of knowledge,
     judgment and wisdom, and is something broader than the societal institution of education we
     often speak of. Many educationalists consider it a weak and woolly field, too far removed from
     the practical applications of the real world to be useful. But philosophers dating back to Plato
     and the Ancient Greeks have given the area much thought and emphasis, and there is little doubt
     that their work has helped shape the practice of education over the millennia.
           Plato is the earliest important educational thinker, and education is an essential element in
     “The Republic” (his most important work on philosophy and political theory, written around
     360 B.C.). In it, he advocates some rather extreme methods: removing children from their mothers’
     care and raising them as wards of the state, and differentiating children suitable to the various
     castes, the highest receiving the most education, so that they could act as guardians of the city
     and care for the less able. He believed that education should be holistic, including facts, skills,
     physical discipline, music and art. Plato’s beliefs regarding education was very democratic in
     that he believed that talent and intelligence is not distributed genetically and thus is be found in
     children born to all classes; however, his proposed system of selective public education for an
     educated minority of the population does not really follow a democratic model.
                                               -2-

         Aristotle considered human nature, habit and reason to be equally important forces to be
   cultivated in education, the ultimate aim of which should be to produce good and virtuous
   citizens. He proposed that teachers lead their students systematically, and that repetition be
   used as a key tool to develop good habits, unlike Socrates’ emphasis on questioning his listeners
   to bring out their own ideas. He emphasized the balancing of the theoretical and practical
   aspects of subjects taught, among which he explicitly mentions reading, writing, mathematics,
   music, physical education, literature, history, and a wide range of sciences, as well as play,
   which he also considered important.
        During the Medieval period, the idea of Perennialism was first formulated by St. Thomas
   Aquinas in his work “De Magistro”. Perennialism holds that one should teach those things
   deemed to be of everlasting importance to all people everywhere, namely principles and
   reasoning, not just facts (which are apt to change over time), and that one should teach first
   about people, not machines or techniques. It was originally religious in nature, and it was only
   much later that a theory of secular perennialism developed.
         During the Renaissance, the French skeptic Michel de Montaigne (1533 - 1592) was one
   of the first to critically look at education. Unusually for his time, Montaigne was willing to
   question the conventional wisdom of the period, calling into question the whole edifice of the
   educational system, and the implicit assumption that university-educated philosophers were
   necessarily wiser than uneducated farm workers, for example.

1.explanation: “This past summer” is a finished time in the past, so use the simple past “lost.”

2.explanation: “Since morning” describes an action continuing until now; use the present perfect continuous.

3.explanation: “Now” describes the Commissioner’s current state/desire; “wants” is the simple present. “Commissioner” is singular.

4.explanation: The driving was in progress when the accident happened, so use past continuous.

5.explanation: In a future time clause after “when,” use the present tense; the main clause takes “will call.”

6.explanation: The past perfect uses the past participle “written”: “had written.”

7.explanation: A general scientific fact takes simple present: the earth revolves around the sun.

8.explanation: “By the time you arrive” is a future deadline; the work will have been completed by then.

9.explanation: The present perfect auxiliary “have” takes the past participle “broken.”

10.explanation: After “did,” use the base form “run.”

11.explanation: “Above mine” means on a higher floor; “above” is the appropriate preposition.

12.explanation: “Till Saturday” means continuing up to Saturday.

13.explanation: The idiom is “take a keen interest in” something.

14.explanation: The standard collocation is “respect for” someone.

15.explanation: The standard collocation is “control over” someone or something.

16.explanation: “Into” marks movement from outside to inside the cup.

17.explanation: “Beside” means next to. “Besides” means in addition to.

18.explanation: The adjective “worthy” takes the preposition “of.”

19.explanation: “Behind the fence” means on its far side, which best fits the location.

20.explanation: The standard collocation is “congratulate someone on” a success.

21.explanation: “Therefore” introduces the result of his being sick.

22.explanation: “Whereas” contrasts what wise people do with what fools do.

23.explanation: “So that” introduces the purpose: working hard to keep the family from starving.

24.explanation: “Though … yet” is the conventional concessive pair, even though “though … but” is often avoided.

25.explanation: “Unless” means “if … not”: I will forgive you only if you mend your ways.

26.explanation: “As well as” adds Eric to the subject; the singular main subject “Eric” takes “is.”

27.explanation: “Lest” introduces the feared result, with the sense “work hard so that you do not fail.”

28.explanation: The correlative construction is “not only … but also.”

29.explanation: “While” marks the contrast between his idling and the others’ work.

30.explanation: “Although” introduces a concession: despite the rain, the speaker did not feel cold.

31.explanation: “Worst” is the superlative degree of “bad.”

32.explanation: “Slowly” is the adverb modifying “walk.”

33.explanation: “Coming near” means approaching; “nearly” means almost.

34.explanation: “Work” is uncountable, so “much work” is correct.

35.explanation: “A little water” means a small amount of the uncountable noun “water.”

36.explanation: “Well” is the adverb modifying “performed”; the printed option also supplies the test context.

37.explanation: The sentence needs an adverb modifying “escaped”: “Fortunately.”

38.explanation: “The largest” is the superlative form required by “in the country.”

39.explanation: “Some money” is the natural affirmative request; “money” is uncountable.

40.explanation: “So happy” is the idiomatic degree construction; the negative conveys that he was not very happy.

41.explanation: The participial phrase “Closing the door” replaces the dependent time clause while retaining the main action.

42.explanation: “Whether he may stay or leave” is a subordinate noun clause after “It is not certain.”

43.explanation: The relative clause is reduced to the phrase “by whom my book was stolen,” making a simple sentence.

44.explanation: “So weak that …” converts the “too … to” construction into a complex sentence with a result clause.

45.explanation: “Fortunately” condenses the separate judgment into an adverbial modifier, leaving a simple sentence.

46.explanation: The absolute construction becomes two coordinated main clauses joined by “and therefore.”

47.explanation: The participial phrase “Sensing danger ahead” joins the two events in a simple sentence.

48.explanation: “That she would be successful in the examinations” is a subordinate noun clause completing “hoped.”

49.explanation: “He must work hard, otherwise he cannot pass” joins two independent clauses and preserves the conditional meaning.

50.explanation: “When I reach my office” is a subordinate time clause, producing a complex sentence.

51.explanation: The noun form of “bravely” is “bravery”; “with bravery” expresses the manner.

52.explanation: “Too cheerful to be taken seriously” means “so cheerful that he cannot be taken seriously.”

53.explanation: “Mary is not smarter than John” is equivalent to “Mary is as smart as John” in the comparative transformation.

54.explanation: “Other vegetables are not as healthy as broccoli” expresses the same comparison in the positive degree.

55.explanation: “He did not fail to attend” gives a negative form while preserving the meaning that he attended.

56.explanation: “I long to have …” expresses the wish in an assertive sentence.

57.explanation: “Isn’t virtue its own reward?” is the interrogative form that preserves the original assertion; the source misspells the contraction.

58.explanation: “Strengthened” is the verb that replaces the adjective phrase “made strong.”

59.explanation: “Too urgent to be postponed” correctly transforms “so urgent that it cannot be postponed.”

60.explanation: “Doubtful” expresses the affirmative equivalent of “not sure.”

61.explanation: “If you do not work hard, you will fail the test” correctly joins the condition and result.

62.explanation: “I need a lot of money to start a business” uses an infinitive of purpose.

63.explanation: “A wealthy and generous doctor in our locality” renames Mr. Brown in apposition.

64.explanation: “Diligently” is the adverb modifying “works.”

65.explanation: “Finishing my breakfast” is a participial phrase modifying the subject “I.”

66.explanation: “Until her arms ached” is an adverb clause of time modifying “scrubbed.”

67.explanation: “As well as” is cumulative/additive: she was both miserly and rude.

68.explanation: “That the earth revolves around the sun” is a noun clause serving as the subject of “is a proven fact.”

69.explanation: “Which was stolen from me” is an adjective (relative) clause modifying “shoe.”

70.explanation: “Too noisy to hear” expresses the same result as “so noisy that I cannot hear.”

71.explanation: “Kick the bucket” is an informal idiom meaning to die.

72.explanation: “When pigs fly” describes something that will not happen.

73.explanation: “Set the bar” means establish the standard, here the highest standard for the performances.

74.explanation: “Pay lip service” means profess agreement or support without sincere action.

75.explanation: “Old school” means traditional or conservative.

76.explanation: “Keep someone in the loop” means keep them informed.

77.explanation: “Make light of” means treat something as unimportant or not take it seriously.

78.explanation: “At odds” means in disagreement.

79.explanation: “Light years away” means extremely far off and thus unlikely to happen soon.

80.explanation: A “wet blanket” spoils other people’s enjoyment.

81.explanation: “Penitent” means feeling remorse; “repentant” is its synonym.

82.explanation: “Vengeance” means revenge.

83.explanation: “Revelry” means lively celebration.

84.explanation: “Succulent” means juicy, especially of food.

85.explanation: “Drowsy” means sleepy.

86.explanation: “Fragrant” means pleasantly or sweetly scented.

87.explanation: “Perpetual” means continuing indefinitely; “permanent” is the closest choice.

88.explanation: “Retreat” means withdraw.

89.explanation: “Sensible” means reasonable or prudent; “clever” is the closest offered synonym.

90.explanation: “Gratify” means please or delight.

91.explanation: “Insolent” means rude or ill-mannered.

92.explanation: Calligraphy is the art of beautiful handwriting.

93.explanation: A “philanderer” pursues multiple romantic or sexual relationships, especially with women.

94.explanation: “Zenith” means the highest point or peak.

95.explanation: “Inexorable” means relentless or unstoppable.

96.explanation: “Animated” means lively or energetic.

97.explanation: “Avarice” means extreme greed or love of money.

98.explanation: “Posthumously” means after a person’s death.

99.explanation: “Obsolete” means out of date or no longer current.

100.explanation: “Invincible” means impossible to defeat or conquer.

2.explanation: “Love” names an emotion and is modified by “true,” so it is a noun.

3.explanation: “Herself” is a reflexive/emphatic pronoun referring to “she.”

4.explanation: “Yesterday” modifies when the speaking happened, so it is an adverb.

5.explanation: “Timidly” modifies the verb “enquired,” so it is an adverb.

6.explanation: “Besides money” means “in addition to money”; “besides” is a preposition here.

7.explanation: “Listen” is the verb in “shall not listen.”

8.explanation: “Unless” introduces a condition, so it is a subordinating conjunction.

9.explanation: “Dead” describes the noun “body,” so it is an adjective.

10.explanation: “Past” precedes “the river” and means beyond it, so it is a preposition.

11.explanation: “For two hours” gives a duration continuing to the present; use present perfect continuous.

12.explanation: “Every night” describes a regular habit, so use simple present “prays.”

13.explanation: After modal “could not,” use the base verb “help.”

16.explanation: “It is raining” describes the current reason for not coming.

18.explanation: “Want” is a stative verb normally used in simple present; “the Manager” is singular.

19.explanation: The present perfect auxiliary “Have” takes the participle “written.”

20.explanation: A general repeated event takes simple present: newspapers arrive every day.

21.explanation: “Few questions” is correct with the countable plural “questions.”

22.explanation: “Late” means after the expected time; “latest” means most recent.

23.explanation: “Works hard” means works diligently; “hardly” means scarcely.

24.explanation: “Injurious to your health” is the correct adjective construction.

25.explanation: “Directly” is the adverb meaning straight from the office.

27.explanation: “Circular in shape” describes a round gift box.

28.explanation: “Backwards” is the standard adverb for walking toward the rear.

29.explanation: “Affectionate” is the adjective required after “was very.”

30.explanation: “Aloud” means audibly, so everyone could hear the words.

31.explanation: “Since” introduces the reason it was not possible to come.

32.explanation: “Look up” can mean visit or seek out a person when in their city.

33.explanation: The standard collocation is “control over his temper.”

34.explanation: “Among” is used for distribution to three brothers.

35.explanation: “Lest” introduces the feared consequence: that he might see the speaker looking.

36.explanation: “As if” introduces the comparison of appearance to a possible state.

37.explanation: The comparative adjective “stronger” takes “than.”

38.explanation: The correct construction is “accused of stealing.”

39.explanation: “Onto” marks the frightened woman’s movement to the table’s surface.

40.explanation: “However hard you may try” means regardless of how hard you try.

41.explanation: “Helen is faster” is the main clause; “than Mirren” is the comparison complement.

42.explanation: “Where you lost your wallet” modifies “place,” so it is an adjectival clause.

43.explanation: “That you have succeeded” is the noun clause completing “pleased.”

44.explanation: “When it was night” is the subordinate adverbial clause of time.

47.explanation: “Which most people love” modifies “Pizza,” so it is an adjectival clause.

49.explanation: “Until my arms ached” is an adverbial clause of time.

50.explanation: “Even if it rains” is a subordinate concessive/adverbial clause.

51.explanation: “So loud that I cannot bear it” expresses the result of the excessive loudness.

52.explanation: “The other boys are weaker than Bob” preserves the meaning of “Bob is not as weak as the other boys.”

53.explanation: “Blunt” is the positive-degree equivalent of “not sharp.”

55.explanation: “You are lazy, therefore you are losing” joins two independent clauses with a result connector.

56.explanation: “O that I may see my hometown again!” is the exclamatory wish form.

57.explanation: The noun form of “cruel” is “cruelty.”

59.explanation: “Maths is the easiest subject” expresses the superlative equivalent intended by the options.

60.explanation: “Too sweet to be eaten” is the standard equivalent of “so sweet that it cannot be eaten.”

61.explanation: “Sadly” is an adverb expressing the speaker’s evaluation of the event.

62.explanation: “The beauty of her voice” uses the noun “beauty” for the adjective “beautiful.”

63.explanation: “Having seen the advertisement” is a perfect participial phrase showing the earlier action.

64.explanation: “But” is an adversative conjunction marking contrast; it gives the closest instructed form.

65.explanation: “Whether she may cry or laugh” is the subordinate clause completing “It is not certain.”

66.explanation: “Which is yellow in colour” is the adjective clause modifying “umbrella.”

67.explanation: “As well as” is the cumulative/additive conjunction joining the two things she dropped.

68.explanation: “Too dirty to wear” uses an infinitive to express the result of the dirtiness.

69.explanation: “My sister” is a noun phrase in apposition to “Clara.”

70.explanation: “Closing the window” is a participial phrase modifying the subject “he.”

71.explanation: “Eligible” means qualified or suitable; it fits the idea of being wanted as a spouse.

72.explanation: “Generosity” is willingness to help others.

73.explanation: “Accept” means receive or agree to take; “except” means excluding.

74.explanation: “Loss” is the noun meaning the state of having lost someone.

75.explanation: A “turn-coat” betrays one side by changing allegiance.

76.explanation: An “amateur” is a beginner or nonprofessional.

77.explanation: “Perceive” means become aware of or understand through the senses.

78.explanation: A “mercenary” is hired to fight or kill for payment.

79.explanation: A “hypocrite” does not practise what they preach.

80.explanation: “Calligraphy” is the art or style of handwriting.

81.explanation: “Inevitable” means unavoidable.

82.explanation: “Descended” means moved downwards.

83.explanation: “Verbose” means using many words; “talkative” is closest.

84.explanation: “Sufficient” means enough.

85.explanation: A “virtuoso” is an expert with exceptional skill.

86.explanation: “Conceit” means excessive self-regard or vanity.

87.explanation: “Oblivious” means unaware.

88.explanation: “Discreetly” means carefully and tactfully; “cautiously” is closest.

89.explanation: “Fortitude” means courage in difficulty.

90.explanation: “Peril” means danger.

91.explanation: “Peculiar” means unusual or strange.

92.explanation: “Apathy” means lack of interest or concern; “indifference” is its synonym.

93.explanation: “Imperious” means domineering or overbearing; “proud” is the closest choice.

94.explanation: “Decisive” means firm and determined.

95.explanation: “Enmity” means hostility; “fighting” is the closest offered choice.

96.explanation: “Dexterity” means skill, especially with the hands.

97.explanation: “Solidarity” means unity or agreement within a group.

98.explanation: “Accursed” means cursed or hateful.

100.explanation: “Affable” means friendly and easy to talk to.

17.passage: Everything that men do or think concerns either the satisfaction of the needs they feel or the need to escape from pain. This must be kept in mind when we seek to understand spiritual or intellectual movements and the way in which they develop, for feeling and longing are the motive forces of all human striving and productivity—however nobly these latter may display themselves to us. What, then, are the feelings and the needs which have brought mankind to religious thought and to faith in the widest sense? A moment’s consideration shows that the most varied emotions stand at the cradle of religious thought and experience. In primitive people it is, first of all, fear that awakens religious ideas—fear of hunger, of wild animals, of illness and of death. Since the understanding of causal connections is usually limited on this level of existence, the human soul forges a being, more or less like itself, on whose will and activities depend the experiences which it fears. One hopes to win the favour of this being, by deeds and sacrifices, which according to the tradition of the race are supposed to appease the being or to make him well disposed to man. I call this the religion of fear. This religion is considerably established, though not caused, by the formation of priestly caste which claims to mediate between the people and the being they fear and so attains a position of power. Often a leader or despot will combine the function of the priesthood with its own temporal rule for the sake of greater security; or an alliance may exist between the interests of political power and the priestly caste.

One hopes to win the favour of this being, by deeds and sacrifices, which according to the tradition of the race are supposed to appease the being or to make him well disposed to man. I call this the religion of fear. This religion is considerably established, though not caused, by the formation of priestly caste which claims to mediate between the people and the being they fear and so attains a position of power. Often a leader or despot will combine the function of the priesthood with its own temporal rule for the sake of greater security; or an alliance may exist between the interests of political power and the priestly caste.

28.q: Which statement about harnessing energy from sea waves is correct?

opts.d: It results in saving of useful land area.

28.passage: According to the research findings of a team of American scientists published recently, the sea waves contain as much energy as the world is consuming at present. Scientists have found that through the application of two major devices called land-based systems and offshore devices, this source of energy can provide huge amount of electricity without cooling towers and pollution. Land-based systems include tapered channels and fixed Oscillating Water Column (OWC) devices, whereas offshore devices include floating OWC devices, buoys, etc. Through these devices the mechanical energy of ocean waves is absorbed and converted into electrical energy. The wave power potential depends on numerous factors such as the device’s capability to harness long wavelengths, period of waves and depth of water where they arise. Compared to conventional power stations which require greater space and are difficult to maintain in critical situations, wave power devices are highly modular, cost effective and easier to upgrade. As recent findings suggest, sea wave energy has much greater potential to be used for electricity generation than the hitherto known sources of renewable energy. Moreover, most renewable energy systems require hundreds of square acres of useful land for their installation. But in case of wave energy devices, “space crunch” can never be a serious problem.
