17.q: Manners may be defined as:

opts.a: success in playing one’s role in society
opts.b: how we act when we are at home

17.passage: Man is a social animal. But living in society is not an easy job. There are social codes of conduct to be followed if one is to live in civilised society. How one behaves with others, how he approaches another person and how far he is successful in playing his role in the society indicates his manners. So, broadly speaking, we can define manners to be well established standard of conduct on the social life. Nobody is born with inherent good manners. Everyone either learns or acquires them. The best place to cultivate manners and etiquettes is the home which is a miniature society and where the child spends most of its time. Children try to imitate their parents and elders in their behaviour and slowly learn and acquire certain traits of character that they have learnt at home. In the school, the teacher plays an important role in cultivation of good manners and etiquettes. Teachers with their ideal behaviour imbibe good manners in the school students. Anywhere we go, we are judged by the way we speak because it is a good indicator of our character and personality. How we speak, both to people who are younger and older than us, reflects our personality. More than anything, our manner of speaking to people who are socially inferior to us speaks a great deal about our character. The well-mannered person interacts with everyone in the same polite manner, regardless of age, sex, class, gender or religion. He does not discriminate, but respects each individual regardless of their status. He always tries to avoid offensive and harsh words and always shows respect to others. It is also equally important to be very careful about one’s behaviour in any social gathering. Not only our words, but our action and gestures should also be polite. Polite actions include opening doors for others, greeting them, giving up our seats in public transportations, not encroaching on their personal space, etc. Give everybody an equal opportunity to speak and never try to speak while another person is speaking. Respect the person who is speaking. Do not get agitated if one does not agree with you or when you disagree with others. In a group of people always wait for your turn to speak. Do not monopolise the whole conversation. If ever you want to criticise anybody, do it in a manner that it does not hurt the person. Do it in a polite and civilised manner. It has often been said that ‘manners maketh man’. It is good manners that define us as civilised persons. We judge people based on their words and actions and the polite, well-mannered individual is immediately perceived as mature, confident and capable. One may amass great wealth or fame, but if his manners are unpleasant, he does not command respect. Therefore, if one wants to be considered as a respectable and confident person, he first has to treat others in a respectable manner. By cultivating good manners, one can thereby, become the person that he wishes to be.

Anywhere we go, we are judged by the way we speak because it is a good indicator of our character and personality. How we speak, both to people who are younger and older than us, reflects our personality. More than anything, our manner of speaking to people who are socially inferior to us speaks a great deal about our character. The well-mannered person interacts with everyone in the same polite manner, regardless of age, sex, class, gender or religion. He does not discriminate, but respects each individual regardless of their status. He always tries to avoid offensive and harsh words and always shows respect to others. It is also equally important to be very careful about one’s behaviour in any social gathering. Not only our words, but our action and gestures should also be polite. Polite actions include opening doors for others, greeting them, giving up our seats in public transportations, not encroaching on their personal space, etc. Give everybody an equal opportunity to speak and never try to speak while another person is speaking. Respect the person who is speaking. Do not get agitated if one does not agree with you or when you disagree with others. In a group of people always wait for your turn to speak. Do not monopolise the whole conversation. If ever you want to criticise anybody, do it in a manner that it does not hurt the person. Do it in a polite and civilised manner. It has often been said that ‘manners maketh man’. It is good manners that define us as civilised persons. We judge people based on their words and actions and the polite, well-mannered individual is immediately perceived as mature, confident and capable. One may amass great wealth or fame, but if his manners are unpleasant, he does not command respect. Therefore, if one wants to be considered as a respectable and confident person, he first has to treat others in a respectable manner. By cultivating good manners, one can thereby, become the person that he wishes to be.

1.explanation: “Degenerate” modifies the noun “gambler,” so it is an adjective.

2.explanation: “Beauty” names a quality and is the subject of “caught,” so it is a noun.

3.explanation: “None” stands for no person other than the Queen and functions as a pronoun.

4.explanation: “Leave” is the action the visitors are permitted to perform, so it is a verb.

5.explanation: “Upon” links “rock” to the relative clause and functions as a preposition.

6.explanation: “Though” introduces a concessive dependent clause, so it is a conjunction.

7.explanation: “Steadily” modifies “persevered,” so it is an adverb.

8.explanation: “Still” means “nevertheless” and modifies the following clause as a conjunctive adverb; the matching part of speech is adverb.

9.explanation: “Lo!” is an interjection expressing surprise or drawing attention.

10.explanation: “Glorious” modifies “sunrise,” so it is an adjective.

11.explanation: The habitual action takes the simple present: “She goes to school daily.”

12.explanation: “Neither … nor” with singular subjects takes a singular verb; “yesterday” requires past “was.”

13.explanation: “By the time we finish” sets a future deadline, so future perfect “will have reached” fits.

14.explanation: The swim was in progress when the shark attacked; use past continuous.

15.explanation: “Previously” marks an earlier past event, so past perfect “had seen” fits.

16.explanation: “Will see you now” is the natural future offer/appointment formula.

17.explanation: “Since” marks a starting point and the sitting continues to now, requiring present perfect continuous.

18.explanation: “Yesterday” requires simple past “saw.”

20.explanation: Finishing occurred before the phone rang, so past perfect “had finished” fits.

21.explanation: The idiom is “agree with each other.”

22.explanation: “Look into” means investigate the matter.

23.explanation: The standard collocation is “convinced of his guilt.”

24.explanation: “Venture beyond the gates” means go outside their limits.

26.explanation: “Since nine months back” gives the starting point of a period continuing to now.

28.explanation: A stream running beside a shack runs alongside it; “besides” means in addition to.

29.explanation: A specific intersection/crossroads is located with “at.”

30.explanation: “Look after” means care for the children.

31.explanation: “Shall arrive” is simple future (future indefinite), not a perfect or continuous form.

32.explanation: “Have seen” is present perfect: have + past participle.

33.explanation: “Will have sold” is future perfect.

34.explanation: “Have been seeing” is present perfect continuous.

35.explanation: “Did … see” is simple past, or past indefinite.

36.explanation: The verb “rained” is modified by the adverb “steadily.”

37.explanation: The noun “difficulty” follows “great”; the other forms do not fit this noun phrase.

38.explanation: The adjective “great” modifies “display.”

39.explanation: “Whose” asks who owns the jacket.

40.explanation: “Later this evening” means at a subsequent time this evening.

41.explanation: The superlative claim is restated as “No other boy … is as good as him.”

42.explanation: The sentence says serving in heaven is not as desirable as reigning in hell.

43.explanation: If no other employee is as lazy as you, you are the laziest.

44.explanation: The superlative “most expensive” is restated by comparison with every other area.

45.explanation: Having more contacts means you do not have as many contacts as I do.

46.explanation: “Is it a waste of time asking him for help?” is an interrogative version preserving the claim.

47.explanation: “She is a lovely person” restates the exclamation as an assertive sentence.

48.explanation: “Everybody will admit his right” expresses positively the meaning of “Nobody will deny his right.”

49.explanation: “Bring me a cup of tea” is the only imperative form among the options, though it changes the polite request to a command.

50.explanation: “Pooh! What a dirty fellow!” is the exclamatory construction.

51.explanation: “He was ill and could not attend school” joins the clauses with “and,” producing a compound sentence.

52.explanation: “You have committed a crime, therefore you are suffering” joins the cause and result as independent clauses.

53.explanation: “As he overworked himself, his health broke down” uses a subordinate causal clause, making a complex sentence.

54.explanation: “If you speak the truth, you will be forgiven” expresses the condition and result as a complex sentence.

55.explanation: “But” joins the contrasting independent clauses in a compound sentence.

56.explanation: “With all his great learning” is a phrase replacing the concessive clause, yielding a simple sentence.

57.explanation: “Though he is wealthy, yet he is not happy” converts the concessive phrase into a dependent clause.

59.explanation: “The sun rose and we returned to the house” joins two independent clauses with “and.”

60.explanation: “Do as I say or you will not succeed” expresses the “unless” condition as an alternative.

61.explanation: “We shall not succeed unless we work hard” preserves the original conditional relation.

62.explanation: “Who is in a grey suit” is a relative clause describing “the man.”

63.explanation: The “as well as” phrase takes agreement with the first subject “John”: “John … has committed.”

65.explanation: “But” is an adversative conjunction joining the contrast between hard work and lack of brightness.

68.explanation: “Not only Amos but also Abel participated” correctly pairs the correlative conjunctions and keeps a plural subject.

69.explanation: “Unsuccessfully” is the adverb expressing that the attempt to open the door did not succeed.

71.explanation: “All at sea” means completely confused.

72.explanation: A “moot point” is a matter of debate or practical irrelevance; “irrelevant piece of information” is closest among the choices.

73.explanation: “Bury the hatchet” means end a conflict and make peace.

74.explanation: “Lily-livered” means cowardly.

75.explanation: “Dressed in mufti” means wearing ordinary civilian clothes.

76.explanation: To “bring the house down” is to win loud laughter or applause from an audience.

77.explanation: “Flog a dead horse” means keep expending effort on a lost cause.

1.explanation: ‘Sufficient’ modifies the noun ‘rain’, so it is an adjective.

2.explanation: ‘Copper’ specifies the kind of coins and functions as an attributive adjective in the printed choices.

3.explanation: ‘Gentry’ is a noun naming a social class/group.

4.explanation: ‘Strength’ names a quality and is a noun.

5.explanation: ‘While’ joins the main clause to the dependent clause, so it is a conjunction.

6.explanation: ‘Pull’ is the imperative verb, giving a command.

7.explanation: ‘Fast’ modifies the verb ‘build’, so it is an adverb here.

8.explanation: ‘Oh my god!’ is an exclamation expressing a sudden reaction; it is an interjection.

9.explanation: ‘Them’ is an object-form personal pronoun.

10.explanation: ‘Beyond’ takes the noun phrase ‘the boundary of the field’ as its object, so it is a preposition.

11.explanation: The sentence asks a direct question and ends with a question mark; it is interrogative.

12.explanation: ‘Bravo!’ expresses strong feeling; the sentence is exclamatory.

13.explanation: It makes a statement, so it is declarative.

14.explanation: ‘Get out’ is a command addressed to Ravi; it is imperative.

15.explanation: The exclamation mark and exclamatory word order signal an exclamatory sentence.

16.explanation: ‘Please clean’ is a polite command, hence imperative.

17.explanation: It states a fact about the girl; it is declarative.

18.explanation: ‘Oh!’ and the exclamatory construction express a strong reaction.

19.explanation: It asks a yes/no question, so it is interrogative.

20.explanation: It states a fact, so it is declarative.

21.explanation: The construction is ‘sent a watch for me’: ‘for’ marks the intended recipient.

22.explanation: ‘Beneath a large shady tree’ means under the tree; ‘beneath’ is the fitting listed preposition.

23.explanation: The idiomatic construction is ‘the school that she studies in’; the scan’s option (b) reads ‘in’ (OCR rendered it as ‘n’).

24.explanation: ‘With a scissors’ uses ‘with’ to name the instrument.

25.explanation: ‘Beyond my ability to spend’ means exceeding what I can afford.

26.explanation: ‘Considering their all-year performance’ gives the basis for selection.

27.explanation: ‘During our examinations’ identifies the period when they should not disturb each other.

28.explanation: ‘Regarding their likes and dislikes’ means about those preferences.

29.explanation: A memorandum is submitted to a person or authority; ‘to’ is the correct preposition.

30.explanation: ‘Put up with’ means tolerate; the sentence says five puppies are almost too many to tolerate/manage.

31.explanation: The proverb’s paired infinitives express one general subject/idea; the conventional completion is ‘makes a man healthy…’.

32.explanation: ‘Each’ makes the coordinated subject distributive and singular, so the verb is ‘brings’.

33.explanation: With ‘neither…nor’, the nearer singular subject ‘rain’ takes ‘seems’.

34.explanation: With ‘neither…nor’, the verb agrees with the nearer plural subject ‘friends’: ‘were hurt’.

35.explanation: The joined subject ‘you and he’ is plural, so ‘are birds’ is the grammatical option.

36.explanation: ‘A number of boys’ is plural and the sentence is passive: ‘were caught copying’.

37.explanation: ‘A number of suggestions’ is plural, so the present perfect passive is ‘have been made’.

38.explanation: ‘Politics’ is singular in this sense (a field/occupation); the past-tense verb is ‘was’.

39.explanation: ‘A variety of pleasing objects’ refers to multiple objects; plural ‘charm’ agrees with them.

40.explanation: ‘As well as Hari and Govind’ is parenthetical; the singular subject ‘John’ takes ‘likes’.

41.explanation: There is one independent clause and no subordinate clause or second independent clause; it is simple.

42.explanation: ‘Which you are wearing’ is a relative subordinate clause, so the sentence is complex.

43.explanation: It has one independent clause with no subordinate clause; it is simple.

44.explanation: ‘Who lives in this room’ is a relative clause modifying ‘boy’; the sentence is complex.

45.explanation: ‘As well as her sister’ is a phrase, not a clause; there is one independent clause, so it is simple.

46.explanation: The appositive ‘our first Prime Minister’ is a phrase; the sentence has one independent clause.

47.explanation: Two independent clauses are joined by ‘and’, making a compound sentence.

48.explanation: ‘Since I believed his words’ is a subordinate adverbial clause, so the sentence is complex.

49.explanation: Two predicates are joined by ‘but’ and each has its own subject understood/repeated; the construction is compound.

50.explanation: ‘Because the radio was on’ is a subordinate adverbial clause; the sentence is complex.

51.explanation: The construction “as rich as” uses the positive degree of the adjective; the sentence is in the positive degree.

52.explanation: ‘Taller than’ explicitly uses the comparative degree.

53.explanation: ‘Clever’ is in its base (positive) degree; “so…that” introduces a result clause rather than a comparison.

54.explanation: ‘Not destined’ is a negative construction; it is not a comparison degree.

55.explanation: ‘One of the most intelligent’ uses the superlative form.

56.explanation: ‘Largest’ is a superlative adjective.

57.explanation: ‘More useful than’ is the comparative form.

58.explanation: The auxiliary ‘not’ makes the sentence negative.

59.explanation: ‘Biggest’ is a superlative adjective.

60.explanation: ‘So hot as’ uses the positive degree in an equality comparison.

61.explanation: The underlined ‘how impudent the boy was’ functions as the object of ‘remarked’, so it is a noun clause.

62.explanation: ‘Where she was born’ modifies ‘village’ by identifying which village; it is an adjective (relative) clause.

63.explanation: ‘That you are drunk’ is the subject of ‘aggravates’, so it is a noun clause.

64.explanation: ‘When the seeds of character are sown’ modifies ‘time’; it is an adjective clause.

65.explanation: ‘Who is industrious’ modifies the noun ‘man’; it is an adjective clause.

66.explanation: ‘When the cat is away’ tells when the mice will play; it is an adverb clause of time.

67.explanation: ‘As he thinks’ modifies ‘speak’ and expresses manner; it is an adverb clause.

68.explanation: ‘Which is lost’ modifies ‘moment’; it is an adjective clause.

69.explanation: ‘That he could not stand’ expresses the result of being so tired; it is an adverb clause of result.

70.explanation: ‘As the war was ended’ gives the time/circumstance for the soldiers’ return; it is an adverb clause.

71.explanation: ‘Done up’ means exhausted, fitting the result of walking twenty miles.

72.explanation: ‘Brings in’ means yields as income; the building brings in Rs. 5,000 monthly.

73.explanation: ‘Call out’ means elicit or bring forth; new responsibilities can call out latent virtues and abilities.

74.explanation: ‘Come off’ means take place; the question asks when the convocation takes place.

75.explanation: ‘Carry out orders’ means execute or obey them.

76.explanation: ‘Cut off in the prime of life’ means die prematurely.

77.explanation: “Pass by” means overlook or disregard. The simple past is possible with “generally” for a past habitual action; this is the only idiomatically fitting option.

78.explanation: ‘Make out’ means understand or decipher; one can make out the meaning of a verse.

79.explanation: ‘Run up to’ means reach/amount to; the tailor’s bill has run up to a large amount.

80.explanation: ‘Take up room’ means occupy space.

81.explanation: ‘Fatally injured’ means injured so severely that death follows; ‘gravely’ means seriously but does not itself imply death.

82.explanation: ‘Respectable clothes’ means decent/creditable clothing; ‘respectful’ describes a person’s attitude.

83.explanation: ‘Too intelligent to be deceived’ is the natural completion: intelligence makes someone less easily deceived.

85.explanation: ‘Sense trouble’ means detect or anticipate it; the other options do not fit this meaning.

86.explanation: A ‘site’ is a place selected for a building project.

87.explanation: An ‘illusion’ is a false perception or unreal appearance; ‘a world of illusions’ is the idiomatic phrase.

88.explanation: A ‘feat of engineering’ is a notable achievement accomplished through engineering.

89.explanation: ‘Inappropriate’ means unsuitable; it fits ‘grossly ____ to suggest…’.

90.explanation: ‘Impair your judgement’ means weaken or damage it.

91.explanation: A cacophony is a harsh, discordant mixture of sounds.

92.explanation: ‘Meticulous’ means very careful and precise.

97.explanation: ‘Vice’ means immoral conduct or a bad habit.

98.explanation: ‘Disrupt’ means interrupt or throw into disorder.

99.explanation: ‘Illegible’ means impossible or difficult to read; it describes unreadable handwriting.

17.q: The passage is about:
17.direction:
Directions for the following 3 (three) passages: Read the following passages carefully and choose the best answer to each of the questions out of the four alternatives:

Passage – 1 : Questions Nos. 17 – 22
One cannot be truly human and civilised unless one looks upon not only all fellow-men but all creation with the eyes of a friend. Throughout India, edicts carved on rocks and iron pillars are reminders that 22 centuries ago Emperor Ashoka defined a king’s duty as not merely to protect citizens and punish wrong-doers but also to preserve animal life and forest trees. Ashoka was the first and perhaps the only monarch until very recently, to forbid the killing of a large number of species of animals for sport or food. He went further, regretting the carnage of his military conquests and enjoining upon his successors to find “their only pleasure in the peace that comes through righteousness.”
Along with the rest of mankind, we in India – in spite of Ashoka – have been guilty of wanton disregard for the sources of our sustenance. We share your concern at the rapid deterioration of flora and fauna. Some of our own wild life has been wiped out, miles of forests with beautiful old trees, mute witnesses of history, have been destroyed. Even though our industrial development is in its infancy, and at its most difficult stage, we are taking various steps to deal with incipient environmental imbalances; the more so because of our concern for the human being – a species which is also imperiled. In poverty he is threatened by malnutrition and disease, in weakness by war, in richness by the pollution brought about by his own prosperity.
(From Indira Gandhi’s Speech at the UN Conference on ‘Human Environment’, 1972)

23.q: Instead of adapting, an animal:

opts.a: goes around for finding a prey
opts.b: is in need of food and water
opts.c: must find ways to feed itself
opts.d: moves into different habitat from time to time

23.direction:
Directions for the following 3 (three) passages: Read the following passages carefully and choose the best answer to each of the questions out of the four alternatives:

Passage – 2 : Questions Nos. 23 – 27
Sometimes an animal copes with a changed situation, not by adapting to it, but by moving away from it to another location. There, it may still have to adapt, but the type of adaptation may be easier. There are primitive races of man that have attempted to avoid the pressures or changes that civilisation brings. They have had to adjust to living in remote or harsh conditions. Examples are the pygmies of the Congo who have escaped into the thickest jungles which are full of dangers. They have learned to obtain a living there and to cope with wild animals. African bushmen manage to live off the arid Kalahari Desert where there is hardly any other life. Life is tough for the bushmen but they are left in peace. These social adaptations could well lead to biological adaptations over a number of generations, but this is a very slow progress and it is unlikely that any single person would be aware of it taking place.

2.q:
Write a précis of the following passage (15 marks):
Technology now threatens to grow into a system, functioning purely in its own interests without regard for the best interest of mankind. Symptomatic of this is the way in which technology has been driven to evolve a special technique for suggesting to man what he imagines he needs. We might eventually arrive at a stage where man, who should be the beneficiary of modern production, becomes a slave to the productive process. On the one hand, he may buy a car, a television set or a washing machine but he becomes, on the other hand, in the office, at his machine in the factory, at his drawing board, in sales-promotion, or even in the manager’s office, merely a tiny cog in a gigantic organisation. He performs his function and plays his part. The little humanity and individuality he has, must be bought at the price of living to further the aims of others. Instead of being able to participate in lively cut-and-thrust of dealing with his fellow beings, instead of handling matters that concern real people, a modern business man leads a remarkably abstract sort of life. The result is that feeling of “not-belonging”, so often deplored these days in public discussions. It is an inner emotion of modern man who experiences sensations of rootlessness, of belonging nowhere, who feels a stranger in his own backyard. Man’s liberation from the vagaries of nature, the basic task we attributed to technology, has now become, by a strange freak of logic, man’s alienation from nature. And what in its beginning seemed destined to exert a humanising influence on man, now turns out to be brutalising him.
2.explanation: Identify the central argument and supporting points, omit examples and repetition, use your own concise wording, preserve the author’s meaning, and give the précis an appropriate title if required.
